speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is the greatest existential challenge to humanity today.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members have endorsed a Motion last year declaring climate change a global emergency and a threat to mankind; and another Motion this year calling on the Government to advance Singapore's inclusive transition towards a low-carbon society, in partnership with corporates, civil society and the community.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Both Motions received support from all sides of the House.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The world is already experiencing more extreme weather events, from devastating floods in Pakistan, Thailand, Indonesia and Australia, to the record-breaking droughts and heat waves in Europe, China and Africa.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In the absence of more ambitious climate action, the toll on human lives and livelihoods will be massive.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By 2050, it is estimated that climate change could lead to 250,000 excess deaths per year worldwide and reduce global annual output by US$23 trillion – the equivalent of wiping out the gross domestic product (GDP) of the United States.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Recent events – the war in Ukraine, ongoing COVID-19 pandemic – have caused economic hardship and energy shortages throughout the world, casting a dark shadow on climate action.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must press on as climate change does not wait for events to be over.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Countries are gathering in Egypt for the 27th United Nations Climate Change Conference, or COP27, to implement the Paris Agreement goals of capping long-term temperature rise and enhancing climate resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In their latest report released ahead of COP27, the UN Climate Change Secretariat has warned that the world is not on course to meet these targets.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Collectively, we must do better to turn the tide and secure a liveable and sustainable future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singaporeans have shown strong support towards our green transition, as announced by the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our stakeholder consultations show that an overwhelming majority of corporates, non-government organisations (NGOs) and citizens believe that addressing climate change is a key priority.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are making headway in our green transition.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are decarbonising our power sector by increasing solar deployment and harnessing green electricity imports from the region.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our National Hydrogen Strategy was recently unveiled at the Singapore International Energy Week.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are partnering major industry players in the Energy and Chemicals sector to develop needle-moving solutions such as carbon capture and storage.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have enhanced grant support for companies hoping to deploy energy-efficient technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will promote resource circularity in our local industry to further reduce energy consumption and curb emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are greening our public transport operations and expanding the electric vehicle ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And we are venturing beyond our shores and seeking out opportunities for international collaboration on green technologies and carbon markets, to get to net zero.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We need an effective carbon price to activate carbon mitigation solutions that will help us achieve our net-zero ambition.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The carbon price provides an effective policy to motivate emitters to take action to reduce their emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Setting the price at the right level requires careful calibration.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Too low a carbon price will not provide sufficient incentive to make the necessary changes to achieve our emissions target.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Too high a price will make the change too steep, erode competitiveness and destabilise our corporate sector.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The proposed carbon price was set after carefully balancing the environmental, economic and social needs of our country.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have considered the availability of cost-effective green technologies and products, the pace of change we need to have and that our private sector can manage, and the support we need to give our companies and people to cushion the impact where necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: All that with the intention of reaching our net-zero pathway.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Carbon pricing has been implemented in many countries.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Close to 70 jurisdictions worldwide have implemented carbon pricing instruments, covering about a quarter of global emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Major economies, such as the European Union (EU), are driving global convergence through the imposition of carbon border adjustment mechanisms, intending to place equivalent tariffs on imports from countries with low or no carbon prices.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Members from both sides of the aisle have spoken in support of a higher carbon price on multiple occasions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At Budget 2022, the Government announced that Singapore will raise the carbon tax and make a decisive move to achieve our net-zero ambition.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Carbon Pricing (Amendment) Bill will give effect to the key changes announced at Budget 2022 and strengthen our carbon pricing regime.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have decided to raise the carbon tax level progressively in phases and with advance notice, to give our businesses time to plan and carry out their low-carbon transition.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are mindful that our EITE companies will face higher costs than their counterparts in jurisdictions with no or lower effective carbon prices.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These transitory allowances will not offset the entire carbon tax obligation of the EITE companies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It will be limited to only a portion of companies' emissions, help to alleviate near-term competitiveness concerns, and provide a form of support to the companies as they work on reducing emissions and invest in cleaner technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By providing for a transition framework, we minimise the risk of carbon leakage—where companies relocate to another jurisdiction with less stringent climate policies.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Similar frameworks have also been implemented in other jurisdictions with carbon pricing regimes, including the EU, South Korea, and California.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Similar to our corporate income tax framework under the Economic Expansion Incentive (Relief from Income Tax) Act 1967, the industry transition framework will be administered by the Minister for Trade and Industry, who can assign relevant functions and powers to an appropriate public body.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To drive our industry towards becoming best-in-class, the amount of allowances awarded to each facility will be determined based on their performance on specified energy efficiency or carbon intensity benchmarks, or their decarbonisation plans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Companies in non-EITE sectors can continue to tap on support from the Government through broad-based schemes such as the Economic Development Board (EDB)'s Resource Efficiency Grant for Emissions and the National Environment Agency (NEA)'s Energy Efficiency Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The ICCs referred to in the Bill are tradable certificates that represent the reduction or removal of emissions from the atmosphere, generated from projects or programmes outside Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These carbon credits are generated by emissions reduction or removal projects that would not have materialised under a business-as-usual scenario, but are made possible due to financing from carbon markets.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Examples include reforestation projects that sequester more carbon in the atmosphere; or projects that help local communities switch from firewood to cleaner biogas cookstoves, which reduce emissions from current sources.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A robust carbon market which efficiently matches the demand and supply of high-quality carbon credits has multiple benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: One, carbon-emitting companies gain access to an alternative decarbonisation pathway for hard-to-abate emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Two, much-needed finance can be channelled to support emissions reduction or removal projects globally.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Three, these projects can bring valuable co-benefits, such as biodiversity conservation and air pollution reduction.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The development of well-functioning carbon markets is, thus, a vital part of global efforts to get to net zero.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With the finalisation of Paris Agreement Article 6 rulebook at COP26, countries can now cooperate through carbon markets to mutually support their respective climate targets and the raising of global climate ambition.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As an alternative-energy disadvantaged country with limited domestic mitigation potential, Singapore is keenly exploring these new possibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In recent months, we have signed Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with Indonesia, Morocco, Colombia and Vietnam; and exchanged Letters of Intent with Ghana to affirm our shared commitment towards advancing cooperation and capability building on carbon markets.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will step up our efforts to engage more like-minded partner countries with credible climate targets, both in the region and beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Currently, companies only have one mode of carbon tax payment – by surrendering a corresponding amount of Fixed-Price Carbon Credits (FPCC), as referred to in the Bill, purchased from NEA at the prevailing carbon tax level.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill will amend existing sections 2 and 17 of the CPA respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The ICC framework will ensure that the ICC surrendered are of high environmental integrity and compliant with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The new section 33A will stipulate that all ICC surrendered must adhere to a set of eligibility criteria, which will be prescribed in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We intend for our eligibility criteria to minimally reference the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation, or it is more commonly known as CORSIA standards.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These are a set of environmental integrity standards that have been developed and backed by a multilateral process led by the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO), in consultation with green groups and experts, and are widely regarded as some of the most rigorous in the industry.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As the market for carbon credits is nascent and growing, we will review our eligibility criteria periodically to align with developments.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This limit is aligned with other comparable jurisdictions with similar climate ambitions, such as South Korea and California, and ensures that the ICC framework does not diminish the impetus for companies to cut emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will continue to review the facility-level limit over time to align with international developments.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The ICC framework parameters apply only to companies that are carbon tax-liable and are surrendering credits to fulfil part of their carbon tax liabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They do not apply to the voluntary carbon market, where any company can purchase carbon credits to offset their own carbon footprint voluntarily and as part of their corporate climate targets.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill will also update the list of greenhouse gases to keep pace with the latest global developments and refine carbon tax administration.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The list of greenhouse gases and their Global Warming Potential values will be updated in the First and Second Schedules to the CPA, in line with newer standards adopted by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is aligned with the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and its Katowice rulebook, which require all parties to include NF3 in the reporting of their national emissions inventory by 2024.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The inclusion of NF3 will mainly affect facilities in the Electronics sector, but transitional support will be provided to affected companies through grants and incentives, such as the Resource Efficiency Grant for Emissions and Investment Allowance for Emissions Reduction.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Bill will also introduce amendments to improve tax administration.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To minimise unintended gaps in carbon tax collection when there is a transfer in operational control over a taxable facility, the Bill will amend various sections of the CPA to impose revised registration, reporting and payment obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To reduce compliance costs, the deregistration criteria will be expanded to allow companies to apply for deregistration if their facility has ceased operations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In addition, NEA will be empowered to deregister a registered company and facility if the person has wound up, been dissolved, or ceased to exist.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As the carbon tax level is raised from 2024 onwards, the Bill will also prescribe the treatment for the carryover or refund of FPCC purchased at the "old" price and increase the thresholds for waivers of small assessments and appeals to the High Court by a commensurate degree, to simplify administration and minimise the regulatory burden on taxable facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is informed by our principled, balanced approach to carbon pricing and reflects Singapore's unwavering commitment to decisive climate action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This year, through another Motion by the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Sustainability and the Environment, this House called on the Government to partner businesses and Singaporeans to make Singapore a low-carbon society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of us have fought hard to have this ambitious target for many years now and this was a topic I raised repeatedly, and almost annually, in this House.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On a serious note, there is a reason Singapore's net-zero target is such a big deal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore's word is worth its weight in gold, and the world knows it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today's Bill is a testament to that fact.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill raises carbon tax to the levels announced in this year's Budget.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have always said carbon tax is our best weapon against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new rates sharpen this weapon and helps Singapore achieve its net-zero emissions goal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points on how we can continue the push towards a low-carbon society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on companies in EITE sectors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These sectors include the energy, chemicals and electronics sectors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill allows the Government to grant allowances to companies in EITE sectors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In its public consultation, the Government said that these allowances are meant to help such companies "manage the near-term impact on business competitiveness and mitigate the risk of carbon leakage".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do understand that we need to remember the trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We want to push for climate change, but we do not want to push businesses away.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But green groups are concerned, and rightly so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every allowance erodes the coverage of our carbon tax and reduces the urgency to go green.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every allowance weakens the effectiveness of the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points to make on this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, can Minister share how many companies currently belong to the EITE sector and will pay carbon taxes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, how many companies are currently eligible for these allowances?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will the Government decide when to stop granting allowances?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will it consider committing to 2030 as the year by which it will stop granting allowances?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems fair to say that the near term should last no longer than eight years from today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, will the Ministry consider making it a practice to name all companies that receive such allowances from the Government?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no reason these names should be a secret.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are clearly not a matter of commercial sensitivity and companies that do not receive such allowances will rightly wonder whether the Government is secretly granting allowances to their rivals in the same sector.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must not let our carbon tax regime fall under such a cloud of suspicion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point today is on the coverage of our carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is a high proportion, but every percentage counts in the fight against climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At this year's Budget debate, I asked the Government to raise this percentage by lowering the carbon tax threshold to include smaller emitters that are "reportable facilities".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Ministry's position is that lowering the threshold would impose significant regulatory burden and cost on companies, without any meaningful increase in coverage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share how compliance costs would increase for a reportable facility to become a taxable facility?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I mentioned during the debate, operators of these facilities already have to pay the costs of tracking their emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, the only obvious new cost is just the tax itself, and it is precisely my point that they should pay this tax – so that they have an incentive to cut the emissions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point today is on publicising carbon tax data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I previously asked that the Government publish more granular data on the impact of our carbon taxes, such as the trend in emission levels for taxed facilities and the breakdown of revenue by facility type.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government answered by saying that company- and facility-specific data were confidential information that it could not disclose under our Carbon Pricing Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To address this, I suggested that the Government publish a ranking of top emitters without sharing the exact emissions level.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would allow the public to make more informed consumption decisions without compromising business confidentiality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Grace Fu's response was that the Ministry agrees with the need to provide strong impetus for companies to reduce emissions and will continue to study how we can spur this meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share if it will now consider publishing a ranking of top emitters without the exact emissions level?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In summary, I hope that we can clarify and limit allowances granted to EITE companies, expand the carbon tax to all reportable facilities and be more transparent with data on top emitters and ICCs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, we need to remember this quote: "Climate change is sometimes misunderstood as being about changes in the weather.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In reality, it is about changes in our very way of life".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All of us need to change our mindsets and our lifestyles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All of us have an important part to play.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my opening speech for the Climate Change Motion in 2021, I said, "I live this moment with sadness and optimism.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sadness because we are somehow fighting the same battle that our forefathers fought decades ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But also, optimism – because we are now much clearer about what we can do.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Optimism because Singaporeans, more than ever before, are speaking up and taking action".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unfortunately, the sadness continues as each day, we see the effects of climate change right before our very eyes and we feel this change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We see how it may be getting worse and that we are running out of time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us ride on this wave and this growing movement to ensure that we have a healthy planet to live in.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As we debate this Bill, I am proud that our Singapore representatives and youth environmental activists are flying our flag in Egypt at the COP27.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And their participation reminds us of what is at stake here, why this climate change fight is critical, not only for the world but for Singapore's national interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On that note, I would just like to say that I am sure that many Members of the House would agree that all of us owe a profound debt of gratitude to our Singaporean environmental activists who have helped to galvanise public opinion, move the needle and generate very useful ideas for policy debates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the past, Workers' Party Members of Parliament have spoken about how there is scope to raise the carbon tax when comparing Singapore with international benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These are moves in the right direction for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is no greater challenge facing humanity than that of climate change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rising temperatures triggered by growing greenhouse gas (GHGs) emissions in the atmosphere will lead to freakish weather patterns, rising sea levels, rising incidence of heat-related illness, the loss of biodiversity and many other huge, dangerous, and perhaps, irreversible challenges for Singaporeans and for people around the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must avert what is known in economics as the tragedy of the commons – which, in this context, means the problem created when individual countries pursue their national interest in an uncoordinated fashion at the expense of the global environment, leading to disastrous effects applicable to all countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The uniqueness and seriousness of the challenge we face here calls on us to show national resolve and unity across the political spectrum.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If nations do their part, there is every reason to believe that the world can contain the danger posed by climate change.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should remember how nations came together in 1987 to bring into being the Montreal Protocol that succeeded in protecting the ozone layer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That precedent should give us hope that we can avert or, at least, substantially mitigate disaster at the edge of the precipice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Most mainstream economists accept that carbon pricing is probably the most sound and effective approach to controlling emissions of GHGs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Jennifer Morris, research scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), puts it this way: "Rather than regulating exactly where and how emissions should be reduced, carbon pricing gives markets the flexibility to find the cheapest ways to lower emissions." The EU, Japan, China, California and a few other US states are already using carbon pricing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A carbon price, by imposing a tax on large GHG emitters, can potentially result in part of that tax burden being passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But such inflationary pressures need to be mitigated by two means.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is important, not only because we desire social justice, but also because climate change mitigation measures need to be designed to ensure the broadest possible public support, so that the country will continue to back such measures through thick and thin and across political cycles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We do agree that allowances are needed for nationally strategic projects that are important for job creation and job defence, as well as to hedge against needless carbon leakage of large EITE facilities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But we believe that the balance point can be struck a little differently between promoting emissions reduction and ensuring robust support for business using economic incentivisation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In our speeches, we shall explain these amendments in detail and address possible objections.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans want our climate change policies to show ambition and seriousness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is backed up by the recently released results from an online public consultation exercise run by the National Climate Change Secretariat, or NCCS.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some of the suggestions from respondents, such as pivoting away from emissions-intensive industries and doing more to electrify our commercial fleets and vehicle population, have been subjects taken up by the Workers' Party's Members of Parliament in this House in the past, including Hougang Member of Parliament Mr Dennis Tan and Sengkang Member of Parliament Mr Louis Chua, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before leaving this topic, it should be said that the respondents for this consultation contained a disproportionate percentage of younger people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We can, and must generate good jobs from cleaner and greener economic activities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, most of the large multinational companies, or MNCs, in pollutive industries themselves, seeing the writing on the wall, are trying to show that they are transitioning towards greener practices – like refining biofuels rather than crude oil or using carbon capture and sequestration technology, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our challenge going forward is to find ways to promote a serious pursuit of ambitious climate goals with the pursuit of economic ones in tandem, not to counterpose the one to the other.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, in 2021, the Government said in this House that: "Our carbon tax framework has been tailored to our context, putting in place a fair, uniform and transparent price signal to incentivise emissions reductions".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Having said that, the Workers' Party accepts the case for Government allowances vis-à-vis the carbon tax paid by specific entities in principle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This first rationale also applies to economic incentives awarded by agencies like EDB and Enterprise Singapore, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On this note, I would like to ask the Government to expand on the considerations that will come into play in awarding allowances in more detail, a topic treated briefly in section 20D of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, when we consider the question of allowances, there is a difference between carbon tax allowances and general economic incentives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Economic incentives provide benefits that not all firms enjoy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is necessary as the carbon tax is a significant burden applicable to firms and also the wider public.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Imposing this burden comes with a responsibility to ensure that the public and business community see that the burden will be imposed fairly; and exceptions made on a very limited, transparent basis with strong reasons given, as opposed to a perception that allowances are awarded to companies close to any future government for one reason or another, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am not aware if that recommendation is forthcoming at this point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But I shall continue to make the arguments for these amendments —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You can talk about it, and we will address it at the Committee stage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Our amendment (3) in the Order Paper Supplement tackles this problem of having non-time-limited allowances that are not really as circumscribed in scope as they could be, by limiting the number of times a taxable facility can receive allowances.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Assuming that businesses are able to get allowances when they ask for it, our amendment would mean – to take an example – that a facility can obtain allowances in the following years: 2024, 2025, and, if still deemed necessary after a gap, 2029 and 2030, with 2026, 2027 and 2028 being no allowance years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This still leaves a substantial runway for companies to transform to low-emission processes and sources from now until 2026; and leeway for the Government to apply an allowance in 2029 for particularly large and strategic projects, if deemed necessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I would note at this point that large and strategic projects, facilities, factories and so on, typically have breakeven periods and are invested and set up based on projections that go forward far into the future, sometimes 10 years, sometimes 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We believe that lowering the allowance cap makes for a stronger nudge for large emitters to move towards greener business models faster.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We believe that our amendment makes for a better balance point between the competing objectives on the table here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Having said that, I would like to point out that for projects and companies that are deemed to be nationally strategic; or where their business affects the lives of many Singaporeans and they may need more time to transition to greener processes; or we may want to cushion the effects on a wider public, especially vulnerable groups, the Government still has other tools that can be used to address that situation, namely, first of all, other economic incentives that can be applied under other Acts; and secondly, fiscal tools to implement some degree of income redistribution and cushion the effect of higher prices on more vulnerable groups, in a targeted fashion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Our amendments "ensure the award is listed on a registry that is provided free-of-charge and easily accessible to the public through electronic means, specifying..." and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Some members of the public raised this issue during consultations and some study groups as well, and in the Ministry's public response after the carbon tax consultation, the Ministry cited commercial sensitivity concerns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Government has also said it is "not productive or correct" to put companies which pay carbon tax under public scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It could be argued that such awards should remain confidential because their disclosure could give the competitors of the company receiving the award some information that might give them a competitive advantage in the various actions that they choose to undertake; or which might lead to that company being placed in an unfavourable position when negotiating with stakeholders, such as customers and partners, who may ask for better terms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It could also be argued that being publicly known as a recipient of such an award may subject the recipient and their employees to some degree of public opprobrium due to the perception of being on the receiving end of some unfair advantage of some kind.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Or it could be argued that disclosure of awards may hinder the Government in applying different kinds of awards to different companies in consideration of what is needed to close the deal in each case, therefore, making the Government operate at a disadvantage in calibrating the award in each case to the bare minimum necessary to serve the national interest.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There could be other considerations here along similar lines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Companies receiving Government incentives under laws like the Economic Expansion Incentives Act are currently not disclosed, nor, of course, are the amount of the incentives disclosed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why, then, do we call for the carbon tax awards to be disclosed?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And are we calling for the same disclosure for other types of economic incentives?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In fact, there are significant differences between carbon tax allowance awards and more general economic incentives for investment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Hence, it is a lessening of a burden applied to all in the case of one.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: An economic incentive, on the other hand, gives additional benefits to one company that all do not receive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The difference between the two scenarios is that in the first case, a new tax being imposed means new costs to all.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If one entity has their cost lessened, to obtain general buy-in for the tax among all companies and the public, a certain degree of transparency and public accountability is warranted for the new regime to be seen as fair.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Moreover, given that the carbon tax imposes costs across the whole society and an allowance blunts the effect of that tax to some degree, there is a public interest in knowing who receives such awards, to ensure accountability vis-à-vis the goals of the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This helps ensure that any government of the day does not prop up certain companies for an unjustifiably long period of time, or even in perpetuity, for whatever reason.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This ensures public support for a costly tax that is meant to be, in the words of the Government spoken in this House in 2021, a "fair, uniform and transparent price signal" that advances climate change goals; or, to quote the Government's words again in 2018, to create a carbon tax regime that "will apply uniformly to all sectors, without exemption.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This will maintain a transparent, fair and consistent carbon price across the economy."  On a more practical note, not ensuring that transparency is also not a foolproof means of keeping the award information secret.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Such information often gets leaked and shared by word of mouth within the community of persons interested in such things and may breed speculation and undermine confidence in the business environment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Sometimes, Government incentive information needs to be disclosed to some degree in public filings in the company's home country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I shall not explain them in detail but would be glad to take any questions on those.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Another important set of our amendments will be explained later by Sengkang Member of Parliament Ms He Ting Ru.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leon Perera, you will address those in the Committee stage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I fully support our Government's net-zero ambition and the implementation of measures to achieve our goal, including the carbon taxes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is no doubt that our determination to not damage our environment further will provide a good future for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ideally, there should be a level playing field for all on this earth, for every individual, whether one is a big or small economy, a big or small country.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must not forget that we all share the same earth.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we are determined to stick to our environmental protection commitments, we cannot be sure others will do likewise.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There remains a possibility that other countries will continue to resort to the easy way out, in order to make themselves more price competitive.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is the reality of the global marketplace.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If this were to happen, the global carbon emissions will not be reduced despite the loss of local jobs and investments.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the incentives to develop optimal solutions and technology that will result in no additional cost to achieve net-zero carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Government minimise the impact on consumers at the receiving ends?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the time, I explained why the Workers' Party believes that an emissions price of $15 per tonne – targeted by the existing CPA for 2030 – would be inadequate, and why a tax ranging between $58 and $133 would be more tenable, with $100 a ton being a reasonably close-to-median and scientifically-supported benchmark.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we continue to believe that the appropriate level should be higher, we view this as an important compromise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My Workers' Party colleagues Leon Perera and He Ting Ru have proposed two sets of amendments to the Bill, which we view as important safeguards to further enhance transparency and grant additional flexibility to businesses in how they satisfy their carbon commitments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because I am all about practice and not just theory, I wish to speak about transition issues associated with the practical implementation of a carbon tax; in effect, aspects surrounding the amended Third Schedule of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Presumably, there will be subsequent legislation after 2027 to conform with the stated $50 to $80 target.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe that this unnecessarily binds the hands of policymakers to a schedule that could be detrimental to our short-term economic performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is easy to recognise the appeal of a steady increase in the carbon tax: it is gradual, predictable and incremental, thereby affording businesses time and certainty as they adapt to an impending tax increase.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But its unyielding nature may also be its undoing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the increase in carbon taxes to the proposed range is fairly sharp: in just three years, the rate will be one order of magnitude greater than the $5 a tonne currently in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such a significant hike may also appear to be ill-timed, with our economy just exiting a relatively recent technical recession in 2020 and currently struggling to manage global pressures from rising inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is, however, an alternative: allow the carbon tax to vary over time, with the specific rate adapted to the current prevailing state of the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Following standard principles of stabilisation policy, such an optimal tax would strike a balance between safeguarding the economy and jobs, while protecting the environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If the economy is in a recession, God forbid, the tax would be scaled back.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, if the economy is expanding strongly, it should be able to bear a stiffer increase in the carbon tax rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, accurately calling the state of the economy in real time is admittedly a challenge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But modern macroeconomics, along with access to big data, has already made substantial progress on this front, and it is now possible to reasonably gauge where we stand in the business cycle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In addition, modern central banks routinely gauge the extent to which the economy has deviated from its steady state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The European Central Bank, for instance, adjusts member states' budget balances to reflect the contemporary state of the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would be shocked if the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) does not have its own in-house team that performs this very exercise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Using this approach, the tax would adhere to a central rate outlined in the Third Schedule but be up- or down-weighted by the MAS' evaluation of the current state of the economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Does this proposal undermine the case that other taxes, such as the Goods and Services Tax (GST), should not be raised at this point of the cycle?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If anything, the notion of tax policy being sensitive to the state of the economy is entirely consistent with the argument that an increase in the GST next year is also inappropriate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The basic principle is that carbon taxes – like all taxes – should be higher when the economy is growing steadily and lower otherwise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the reason why I had previously argued for a temporary freeze in GST hikes despite the economy presently growing steadily is because other policy levers – in particular, monetary and exchange rate policy, are already acting counter-cyclically.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This implies that the role of fiscal policy should be limited to serving as a moderating ballast.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, we should keep in mind that, unlike carbon taxes which applies to only goods and services that involve carbon in their production and hence, has a narrower impact, the GST is a broad-based tax, which affects nearly all supplies of goods and services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The impact that rising carbon taxes would have on the economy would have correspondingly a more limited scope.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another that explores whether carbon pricing on inflation, finds that it likewise does not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Incidentally, such a time-varying carbon tax need not apply only to this particular transition period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If the Government subscribes to the general principle that a time-varying carbon tax is attractive, the rate can be adjusted every time the Singapore economy experiences an economic weakness and vice versa.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Beyond the instruments of fiscal policy – for which carbon taxation is a part – the Government can also attempt to realign monetary policy toward favouring green initiatives, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means that MAS can assist our transition process in its move toward net zero.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, MAS is no stranger to green initiatives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The MAS chief Ravi Menon has also explained how the MAS is supporting the development of a transition taxonomy – both at home and abroad – and spearheaded a host of other Enterprise Singapore (ESG) initiatives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, the MAS has mostly been engaged in these initiatives as either a convener or a coordinator, under its financial development mandate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My suggestion is that it can affect the transition process even more directly, by embedding green considerations into its day-to-day operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For example, MAS can target its open market operations toward green bonds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the amount of tradable green bonds may be limited, consciously including green bonds in its potential portfolio of securities that it buys and sells when it conducts monetary policy, can assist us in this transition process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This has been a core plank of the Workers' Party manifesto and is premised on the importance of offering financing to pursue internationalisation and digitalisation objectives for, especially, our small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To this, we can now add support for the green transition for SMEs to this list of objectives for a potential EXIM bank.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In an earlier response by then-Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) Minister Lim Hng Kiang's on why the Government did not feel that an EXIM bank was warranted, he stated that existing schemes under International Enterprise Singapore (IE Singapore) were deemed sufficient, without the "attending financial and implementation risks that setting up an EXIM bank would entail".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand such reservations, it is useful to understand why the Workers' Party, along with, in fact, the MTI's own Economic Strategies Committee have called for such a bank.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Export-import banks, along with export credit agencies, finance cross-border projects that the private sector would otherwise shun.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Typically, these are projects that display substantial externalities, which are the costs or benefits that private agents either do not, or cannot, adequately factor into their own private decision-making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such externalities include the risks of political upheaval, or propensity default on loans, or social benefits.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, projects may only be profitable at such a large scale that it is impossible for any single lender to achieve this scale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Existing financing schemes, such as ESG trade loan facilities, credit guarantees, or political risk insurance schemes, do not adequately meet these needs, since they may not garner sufficient financial scale, or entail externalities that simply are not insurable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: EXIM banks have also proven their mettle in times of crisis, preventing complete collapses in trade finance markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: EXIM banks are, therefore, well suited to support green transition objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In fact, many green financing needs, such access to green energy sources, or carbon credit exchanges, are already inherently cross-border in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My Speaker, a carbon tax that better internalises the externalities associated with the use of carbon in our production is undeniably a step in the right direction and one that codifies into law our responsibility to take into account the welfare of future generations and the sustainability of our economic model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But make no mistake: the transition to a lower-carbon economy and eventually to net zero, will be hard.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As challenging as this may be, there is no reason why we should not ease the process as much as we possibly can.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Allowing the carbon tax to dynamically adapt to the state of the economy, as well as introducing additional aspects to our monetary and financial policies that ease the transition process, will go a long way toward ensuring buy-in from those affected by the carbon tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As difficult as it may be for us today, it is perhaps apt to remind ourselves of why we make the sacrifices we do today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is aptly summarised by a saying, frequently attributed to the Native American people, that "we do not inherit the Earth from our ancestors; we merely borrow it from our children."

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I have listened very intently to Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And I appreciate his suggestion about making carbon tax vary in time, with the economic situation, with GDP or some projections that is short-term.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I will address that later on in my Second Reading closing speech.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But there is a big chunk in the middle that talks about EXIM bank, that talks about financing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I would just like to clarify, whether he finds relevance of what he said to the Bill that we are moving today.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In what way is MSE, as the Ministry moving this Bill responsible for what you have just said?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As I have explained at the beginning of my speech, the bulk of what I am talking about is about a transition process.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I also look forward to the transformative effect it will have on our economy and our environment.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Energy, along with water and food, are vitals that keep Singapore going.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Losing security of any one of them can incapacitate us within a very short time.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It was not too long ago that we courted some of the largest oil and gas companies to invest heavily into our Jurong Island.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: And Singapore became one of the world's largest petrolchemical hub despite not producing any oil or natural gas.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Besides being a significant contributor to our GDP, it also contributed to our energy security.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We managed to secure our access to oil and natural gas through building up a strong petrochemical ecosystem, that is, industry, supply chain and logistics in and around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to likewise implement a similar strategy to plug Singapore into the production, supply chain and market mechanism ecosystem of hydrogen.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This complex endeavour will require years of planning and execution.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Green hydrogen shows promise, but when will it become ready to replace oil or natural gas is unknown.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: What happens if hydrogen and other alternatives take much longer to become viable?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, how do we balance encouraging the petrochemical sector to transit into a low emission model, against the immediate impact on our economy and energy security?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For decades after our Independence, we have been subjected to frequent threats of having our water supply cut off.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Thanks to technological advancement and the foresight of our leaders, we can technically achieve water self-sufficiency through harvesting our NEWater and Desalination National Taps.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: However, this is only true provided we always have access to energy.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Losing energy security also means losing water security.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Direct import of electricity from foreign renewable sources, such as hydropower from Laos and solar power from Australia, may form a significant component of our total energy supply in the future.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: While the supply source can be diversified, the supply cables will ultimately have to physically pass through the lands and waters of our closest neighbours.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The uninterrupted supply of electricity imports may be subjected to geopolitical risks.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Setting aside Government commitments, global investors and MNCs are already leading the way in factoring carbon emission into their business decisions.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: This will lead to higher demand for renewable energy around the world, including the countries that are exporting or planning to export renewable energy.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: If the source countries do not have sufficient renewable energy supply to meet their domestic demand, they may impose export limits.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's power grid's reliability is one of the important factors that helped us advance as a high-value manufacturing base, as well as a technology and financial hub.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just having access to power, but having stable, uninterrupted and reliable access to power.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: How do we manage potential fluctuations of power supply when a significant part is not "produced" domestically?

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic showed us that low probability and high impact events do happen.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: The transition of our energy supply model into a low emission one while promising and exciting, will be met with many unforeseeable and uncontrollable factors.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is why we are debating amendments to the CPA today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even a more conservative target of two degrees warmer still requires global GHG emissions to peak before 2025 at the latest and to be reduced by a quarter by 2030.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While some decarbonising strategies rely heavily on the development of new technologies, we need to continue to pursue other avenues to ensure that we are properly supporting the green transition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These range from – amongst others – consumer education about necessary lifestyle changes, tackling greenwashing, to ensuring that our financing system is set up to properly, and sustainably, support the shift to a climate conscious economy and also to come up with a carbon pricing regime that equitably balances various considerations that come into play.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, a report fronted by McKinsey Sustainability in January 2022 warned that it is not technology that is the main limiting factor, but it is instead the big shifts in thinking and large-scale financing needed that are far behind schedule.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, precisely because so many of these areas and approaches are relatively new, we must make sure that in our rush to "do something" about the problem, we take a moment to evaluate the effects and consequences of our policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, well-intentioned but ultimately inappropriate policies may turn out to be even more costly to unwind when we are further down the path.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is why we support the move to further refine our carbon tax regime, which is a key prong in a multifaceted approach for our transition to a green economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The largest contribution to Singapore's emissions undoubtedly comes from industry.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while it is industry that has been important for our economy, its decarbonisation is crucial, and our policies should be in place to speed progress and to be transparent along the way.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On this note, I, therefore, wish to seek an amendment to the Bill before us, the text of which is contained in the Order Paper Supplement, for the reasons below.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many Members in this House have spoken on the regime's allowing the surrendering of up to 5% of their taxable emissions and in particular, my Sengkang colleague, Mr Louis Chua during this year's Committee of Supply (COS), asked about what accountability measures will be put in place to ensure transparency and fair implementation of this regime.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How will the Minister decide when to lift the prescribed limit?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Is there a framework to constrain this decision-making process?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have therefore sought to make the amendments, as listing the decisions of the Minister on a public registry will allow both industry players and civil society to observe the use of ICCs over the years and whether particular facilities are over-reliant on the use of ICCs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, the danger of allowing facilities to continuously use ICCs beyond the prescribed limit is that facilities may look to purchase ICCs with low and favourable prices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could mean that the cost of producing emissions is significantly less than the cost of paying tax on emissions, which creates a disconnect between the purposes of carbon tax and the permitted use of ICCs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead of being compelled by the prevailing carbon tax to cut down their emissions, the entity-owning facilities may turn their efforts to purchasing favourable ICCs instead.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The problem is exacerbated by how different ICCs may have different criteria for pricing credits.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The value of credits also changes through rounds of trading between entities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The worth of each credit in a different ICC framework, and at different time periods, is different.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And the entity-owning facilities can exploit these differences to obtain credits that give them the greatest financial advantage.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This defeats the purpose of having a fixed carbon tax that has carefully calibrated increases over the years to discourage emissions and, in particular, to make emissions increasing expensive over time.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, having the public registry listing the Minister's decisions will also be a first step in examining whether the use of ICCs indeed fits its purpose of allowing facilities some leeway in producing emissions only in the near to medium term.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If facilities continue to surrender ICCs for many years beyond the prescribed limit, this indicates that they may not have found a way to reduce emissions adequately to avoid paying carbon tax excessively.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Third, requiring the Minister to state their reasons for granting permission to surrender ICCs beyond the prescribed limit ensures that we are told the reasons for such decisions upfront, reducing the need for unhelpful speculation or even false rumours to take bed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It can also give comfort that the Minister has indeed carefully considered the issue of the surrender of ICCs and respect of each facility.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Note, too, that I have not, in the amendment, asked for a disclosure of the amount surrendered as we recognise the commercial sensitivities surrounding this information, particularly in the market environment that is that is still finding its feet, so to speak.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Code of Practice states that companies must disclose how carbon credits are used towards their climate targets, including "whether or not the current credit is associated with corresponding adjustments by the host and/or by a country".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, there is little further information on the criteria for eligible credits and the ability to verify the carbon-lowering activities of such ICCs is key.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could the Minister let us know when we can expect further details on the prescribed criteria as set out in clause 33A and how are these criteria being formulated?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also precisely because the market for ICCs is still new and highly unstandardised that makes it difficult to quantify, and therefore, their use can be controversial.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, academics and environmental groups are concerned that the use of carbon credits could hinder, delay or even displace environmental efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Key aspects of ICCs have not yet been standardised and robust verification mechanisms have not been developed to be applied uniformly across various markets, unlike in the case of commodities, for example, which are traded using industry-specific standardised contracts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The under-regulation of carbon markets also means that there is a risk for greenwashing, a topic which I will come back to later.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If carbon credits themselves are not rigorously regulated, it may end up hindering emissions reductions by reducing the pressure on regulators and thus, businesses, to aggressively commit to investing in cleaner technologies and to move away from high emissions activities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is also concern that there have been consistent over-estimations of emissions reductions in the past.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Adding to the mix is the difficulty in proving a counterfactual – that is, it is hard to prove that offset programmes made something happen that would not otherwise have happened, regardless of the programme's existence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, in spite all of these, the ICCs continue to have a role to play during the intervening years of our green transition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Limitations of today's technologies mean that hard-to-abate sectors still find it difficult to eliminate emissions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While costs may drop as we continue to work on better and cheaper technology solutions, high-quality ICCs are a way for businesses to plug the gap in the meantime.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our emissions reduction pathway to the 1.5-degree warming target still requires carbon offsets to play a role.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Because of the above reasons, ICCs cannot be the only tool in our market's toolkit to facilitate the green transition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some of the lessons learnt and concerns from the green and sustainability financial markets are also useful when we look at ICCs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I note that closer to home, MAS has been making efforts to grow the size of the market here in Singapore and to improve both accessibility to SMEs, and also to maintain an eye on sustainability credentials.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Green financing and the development of robust and large financial markets for green instruments play a very important role to support enterprises and economies towards a decarbonised future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Various financial institutions have been active in developing these markets and various banks have committed to contributing large amounts to sustainable financing and investment by 2030.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Green instruments, like sustainability linked bonds, or SLBs, are ways in which businesses can get access to financing for investment and other activities, which are ostensibly for the purpose of transitioning to more sustainable activities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, the nature of the market at the moment means that companies, the borrowers, pay experts and consultancies should set appropriate sustainability targets and to evaluate these during the course of the bond, to check whether these targets are being met.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Lenders or arrangers, too, would like to be able to announce that they have a large amount of green loans or bonds on their books.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, all three parties benefit by being able to tell their involvement in green financing deals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This leaves a question about whether there is sufficient pressure and whether there is enough independent oversight be exercised to lower the risk of greenwashing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Compounding the problem is that the structure of these green instruments may not have enough negative incentives to make issuers do all they can to meet the sustainability targets set.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while it is true that there are attempts to create standards for sustainability and green targets that issuers and borrowers are expected to meet, such attempts are often voluntary in nature, like the International Capital Market Association (ICMA)'s Green Bond Principles and Sustainability-linked Bond Principles, and they do not address the lack of common disclosure frameworks for each asset class of green instruments and the technical nature of the green or sustainability data points themselves make it open to uncertainty.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, taxonomies, like the ASEAN Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance are still works in progress and it is not clear if they will be voluntary or compulsory.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This lack of meaningful standardisation and uncertainty means that green financing is particularly vulnerable to greenwashing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The private nature of green loans, compared with bonds which tend to be public instruments, also makes it difficult for good data to be readily available to understand the picture more clearly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is against this backdrop that I believe an EXIM bank can really come into its own.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleague from Sengkang, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, earlier mentioned how an EXIM bank can play its role in developing green financial markets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The EXIM bank, having a direct role as a lender or arranger has the added benefit of knowing exactly what the terms of its loans and instruments are.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It can also have a special focus on providing financing options for the research of newer and cheaper green technologies, especially those which are more applicable to the specificities of Singapore and the region's energy and industrial needs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, the bank would also have access to commercially sensitive information like the exact terms of its covenants, when they are breached or require waivers, and will naturally have harmonisation of disclosure built in.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It will also be a natural complement to Project Greenprint's aims of addressing the data challenges of gaps in green and sustainability financial markets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Likewise, we can also ensure that having another effective tool in the box by developing high-quality green financial markets and instruments, which have consistently good standards applied to ensure that the possibility of greenwashing is much reduced.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will go ways to ease the transition to a less carbon intensive world.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must continue to pursue real decarbonisation, in order to ensure that irreversible warming does not become the reality for our planet's future.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.14 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.56 pm until 3.14 pm.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I declare that I am working with a Singaporean bank, but I do not manage any revenue performance target.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Impacted stakeholders include large emitters, SMEs and consumers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What role does Singapore intend to play on the regional and global stage in maintaining our competitiveness and supporting a just transition?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The step towards progressively higher carbon taxes is a bold move.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While doing so will create new opportunities with exciting potential, it has its trade-offs too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On one hand, we want to strengthen our response to climate change because of our island's own vulnerability.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We also aspire to become a carbon services hub in the future, which will attract investments and create job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, the trade-offs include rising business costs and the squeeze on the profits of our companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As an economy with exports constituting more than 170% of our GDP, we risk hurting our international competitiveness with the imposition of such substantial carbon taxes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our trading partners may turn to competitors which, with lower or no carbon tax, can underprice us.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Higher carbon taxes will certainly drive us towards a greener economy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, in view of Singapore's constraints, we must take care to set rates and pace the increases such that businesses will have sufficient time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, I understand and support the Government's decision to provide allowances to large emitters as part of the transition framework.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time that we support the transition of hard-to-abate sectors, we must also ensure that our policies reflect the appropriate level of ambition to maintain Singapore on its decarbonisation pathway.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How many of these large emitters are already complying with these internationally recognised efficiency standards?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If they are already complying, are we not subsidising them by providing them with allowance?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will these large emitters be prescribed a timeline to decarbonise?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the unused allowances be traded in the carbon exchange market?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
