text: Large emitters in Singapore which plan to shrink their carbon tax bills by buying ICCs will be able to do so only if the credits meet Government's prescribed criteria.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At minimum, for instance, the credits must be certified by the Verra or Gold Standard.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government work with Verra and Gold Standard to include local projects in Singapore, or consider the inclusion of Singapore Index on Cities Biodiversity score to generate and offer the carbon credits to emissions-intensive sectors, such as the petrochemical industry, that find it hard to reduce their carbon emissions in the short term?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will stand to benefit both Singapore and the companies that choose to invest in our companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Allowing large emitters to buy credits will also help fulfil Singapore's ambition to become a hub for regional carbon credits.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By prioritising the reduction efforts of domestic emissions, and then allowing large emitters to buy credits, we create a win-win situation for our climate and our carbon market development.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Ministry sharing greater detail how this will be done, as the broad tax will trickle down and find its way to everyone of us?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, will there be an efficiency grants to spur SMEs with their decarbonisation efforts or carbon dividends for the lower-income households?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Singaporeans and our local companies should embrace the opportunities that come with this green transition.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many companies share Singapore's goal of decarbonising and are aligned with its net-zero vision.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their anchor buyers may also require them to commit to net zero.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Efficiency grants can be extended to more companies and industries to ensure that carbon abatement is an economy-wide project.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Tax exemptions could be granted for startups and joint ventures that specialise in emerging green technologies and services.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government should also continue to incentivise green financing initiatives by financial institutions with even greater focus on transition industries in the SME segment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The implementation of carbon tax will catalyse our local SMEs' effort to reduce carbon emission as these companies contribute Scope 3 emission to their supply chains.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is really challenging for them as they will have to follow an accounting methodology that requires knowledge and understanding of the types of business activities contributing to carbon emissions calculations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fees for auditors to assess the outcomes of the calculations and transition costs are essential.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It does require a certain level of rigour and demonstration of that rigour to be able to identify the investments needed to decarbonise and for SMEs to join the net-zero ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The setting of a carbon tax also allows the opportunity for us to examine complimentary policies which will support our nation's decarbonisation goals through regulation, supporting growth of green opportunities and taking a leadership role in ensuring a just transition for the region whilst maintaining our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since reducing our carbon footprint is the main objective, carbon taxes must be complemented by more stringent environmental regulation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The point is not to collect a lot of carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Rather, tight regulations and effective enforcement will deter environmentally harmful behaviours, so that the carbon tax need not do all the heavy lifting.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over time, we will gradually phase out habits, lifestyles, items and systems which are not green.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the large emitters are already applying their own internal carbon prices and are aligned on decarbonisation, I believe that the carbon tax should not have too much of an impact on Singapore's competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although, in the near term, this is a concern because not many countries have a carbon tax to begin with.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, the European Union had unveiled its draft scheme to target imported steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser and other greenhouse gas-intensive goods produced in countries with weaker climate policies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The rationale is to protect the industries in Singapore, which face high carbon costs and progressively tougher climate regulations at home, against cheaper imports from nations with weak or no emissions regulations.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The aim is to try to get everyone on board in terms of putting a cost on carbon dioxide emissions and level the playing field for international trade.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should ensure that the large emitters in Singapore do not set up shop in neighbouring countries with lax climate policies, which make the goods produced there cheaper.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Of course, we are aware that Singapore's competitiveness is not due to tax rates alone, but our entire business ecosystem and high-quality workforce.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the "Transition Finance Towards Net Zero Conference" which was held on 4 October 2022, Senior Minister Tharman mentioned, and I quote, "we need all instruments of public policy to accelerate action".

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need MAS to incentivise and guide the financial institutions to provide transition finance to these large emitters which will try its best to nullify its GHG emissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need ESG to provide more assistance to SMEs so that they know how to measure emissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And we should look to MAS to lead a regional effort to support a just transition and decarbonisation not just in Singapore, but in the region.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Being a frontrunner in adopting sustainable initiatives also means that Singapore companies will be in a better position to help others in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The entire ecosystem of players – Government, regulator, companies, financial institutions, SMEs and consumers need to come together to support our net-zero target by 2050.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope Singaporeans will come together on this issue of greening our economy and focus on the big picture at this inflexion point in our history.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These changes are all the more significant in light of COP27, which is happening right now as we speak, in which I hope and trust that nations around the world will take urgent and decisive action to tackle the existential threat that is climate change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Before I move on to specifics of the Bill, I would like to recognise the Government for setting a net zero by 2050 target, as opposed to the "by or around mid-century" target that was released in Budget 2022 earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I shared in my speech on the Environmental Protection and Management (Amendment) Bill last year and reiterated during the Budget debates this year, we need to set bold, ambitious and specific emissions reduction targets that align with the global goal of reaching net zero by 2050.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The IPCC's sixth Assessment Report, or AR6, makes clear that the world faces a frightening future, even if – and that is a big if – the global economy is decarbonised rapidly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Across all scenarios considered by the IPCC, global temperatures will continue to increase until at least the mid-century.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, we are now expected to reach this 1.5 degree celsius tipping point 10 years earlier than expected.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To limit warming to 1.5 degree celsius with no or limited overshoot, net global CO2 emissions need to fall by about 45% from 2010 levels by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Unless immediate, rapid and large-scale action is taken to reduce emissions, the average global temperature is likely to reach or cross the 1.5 degree celsius warming threshold within 20 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to the specifics of the Bill, the key point I wish to make today is the need for transparency, as well as the need for continued, or even stronger climate ambition.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My first point is on the carbon tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, shared in his speech in February 2021 about the importance of a well-functioning carbon tax system for delivering effective reductions in our nation's carbon footprint.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And as highlighted by some participants who took part in MSE's public consultation, whom, I quote, "were in favour of a more aggressive carbon tax trajectory, citing the higher carbon prices in some other developed countries, the latest scientific recommendations… and the need to sufficiently deter greenhouse gas emissions from growing." As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said at the Singapore International Energy Week recently, the carbon tax is an "important lever to shape responsible behaviour", so that consumers and businesses internalise the costs of carbon emissions in their consumption and investment decisions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our proposed US$35 to US$57 by 2030 still sits below or at the very lowest end of these recommendations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Next, I will touch on the industry transition framework.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party believes in the principle of allowances, and this will be important to ease the transition for both carbon emitters and for individual Singaporeans, such as in the context of a higher carbon tax on power prices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This transition framework could mitigate the impact of higher carbon taxes, such as by giving companies in EITE sectors more time to invest in cleaner technologies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, we must ensure that we do not give out a free meal to polluters.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The introduction of allowances goes against the spirit of the Government's previous commitment to apply the carbon tax uniformly to all sectors, including energy-intensive and trade-exposed sectors, without exemption.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is why we are proposing that the Government publicly disclose which facilities are receiving allowances, and for which emission years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that the Government is proud of the achievements of our energy and chemicals industry, with Singapore ranking as one of the top 10 global chemicals export hubs and one of the top five refinery export hubs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, such a framework could be seen by some that the Government is overly protective of these industries in the face of the existential threat of climate change and with many of these very same companies keen to decarbonise themselves!

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Shell and BP, for example, have set net-zero commitments by 2050.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While ICCs hold significant promise, current markets are still highly unstandardised.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This effectively gives the Minister unlimited legal power to decide the use of ICCs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How will the Minister decide when to lift the prescribed limit?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is there a framework to constrain this decision-making process?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Earlier this year, during the MSE COS debates, I asked about accountability measures to ensure transparency and fair implementation in the use of "high-quality international carbon credits".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the spirit of transparency and accountability, my Sengkang colleague Ms He Ting Ru has filed an amendment to clause 29 for public disclosure of Ministerial decisions to permit registered persons of taxable facilities to surrender eligible ICCs in excess of the prescribed limit.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Before I conclude, Mr Speaker, I would like to touch on the recent US Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I shared in my previous speech about how in 1961, Shell built an oil refinery on Pulau Bukom, and this became one of the largest refinery complexes globally and sparked the start of Singapore's pursuit of the petrochemicals industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the same way, clean energy and green finance can be our next growth sector.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This could have far-reaching effects across industries and supply chains, with companies likely needing to rethink and recalibrate their strategies to not miss out on the opportunities arising from the energy transition.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We need to change the narrative from one of risk mitigation and protection for the industries of the past, to opportunity capture and setting the stage for future growth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our pathway to net zero must be transparent, fair and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As highlighted in public consultations, Singaporeans want to participate in meaningful discourse over our collective future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This can only be achieved if data related to our emissions – and emitters – is made more accessible and available.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The increased ambition in our Carbon Pricing Bill today is welcome, but as climate scientists have repeatedly warned, we are running out of time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is also concerning that while we have a net zero by 2050 target, which is contingent on technological advances, the economic viability of low-carbon technologies and effective international collaborations in areas such as carbon credits and renewable energy imports, it appears that our near-term emissions are still expected to continue accelerating.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise from the Minister's reply to the Parliamentary Question earlier today that we are expected to peak emission sometime between 2025 to 2028, but would that also mean that we are on the higher emissions path in the near term, and are in fact producing even more CO2 than what we previously projected?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At COP27, nations around the world are being urged to cut emissions by 45% by 2030, compared to 2010 levels.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We cannot, in good conscience, continue to release even more carbon dioxide into the atmosphere against this backdrop.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us be that bright green spark and show the world that even in spite of our constraints, Singapore can, and must, strive to do more for the climate.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: According to the World Bank, "A carbon tax reflecting the social cost of carbon is viewed as an essential policy tool to limit carbon emissions".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: All of Singapore needs to support Government to do the right thing, and the right thing to do is to price carbon meaningfully so as to motivate decarbonisation and reduction of CO2 emission.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While the world seems to have come around at COP26 with collective strong intentions to mitigate climate change, the policies and actions taken across countries differ widely.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This leads to the challenge of carbon leakage where companies shift their operations to jurisdictions where there are less stringent rules and taxes on carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially so as the large emitters are key contributors to Singapore's GDP and Singapore's position as an important node in the global value chain of those industries and their ecosystems.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In my speech this afternoon, I would like to tackle three aspects related to the carbon tax: (a) the transition framework; (b) the ICC framework; and (c)	the implementation plan for the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As part of the Bill amendment, there will be a transition framework to support companies to move to low-carbon operations.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Most of the companies in the affected industries, large emitters especially, are already working on decarbonisation and many have pledged to get to net zero by 2050 or thereabout.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these companies, being MNCs, probably have already applied a shadow carbon price or an internal carbon price for their own projects and, therefore, understand and support the need for a meaningful carbon tax in Singapore in order to motivate industry to reduce emission.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding industry's understanding and support, I would like to table the following issues for the MSE's consideration.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Industry players believe that there is a need for a differentiated emission allowance, both in terms of amount and timing, taking into account the specific industry and organisation's decarbonisation plans to achieve low-carbon operations.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There is a thinking that carbon tax pricing should be based on the principle that it is pegged close to the abatement cost, so as to motivate the industry to implement abatement without losing competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next, the industry hopes that the transition framework will consider technology allowances, since countries and industries are all relying on future technologies such as carbon capture and utilisation and storage (CCUS), green hydrogen or nuclear just to name a few.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These technologies are immature and are still in development.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With current technologies, there will still be remnants of carbon remaining and the tax amount can be significant.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am given to believe that current technology is at best 90% efficient, and power and natural gas are still required for burn abatement.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Industry believes that this carbon should be "forgiven" or returned as allowances for the industry to invest into technology development to achieve zero carbon.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe the allowances might even be pooled together to accelerate the development of the future technologies at a macro level.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The third issue concerns indirect carbon tax from electricity.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore power rate is amongst the highest across countries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed carbon tax potentially increases power rates further, and industry has no control over it.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Companies think that they should not be penalised from the lack of green energy in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Industry hopes that further allowance be factored into the transition framework while Singapore is building its green energy infrastructure, and carbon tax resulting from the lack of green energy, should not pass through to industry during this period.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Another side-point is to protect local industrial competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Will we be advocating similar CBAMs with our trading partners and ASEAN?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that real emission reduction should be pursued before carbon credits can be used.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Government's effort to manage and control carbon credit to ensure quality of the carbon credit to be used to offset carbon tax is applaudable.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I believe there is an opportunity for the Singapore Carbon Credit Registry to help to govern and ensure good quality carbon credit for the world, perhaps, by providing a list of accepted ICCs, providing a clear criteria and assessment for qualified projects.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, I do have some questions which I hope MSE can clarify.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What are the Government's plans to enhance the population's understanding of the opportunities and pitfalls of using carbon credits to meet the net-zero emissions target by 2050 and carbon tax obligations under the CPA, especially for carbon credits sourced from nature-based carbon projects that may have far-reaching implications for the climate, biodiversity and local communities?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Earlier on, I had filed a Parliamentary Question about the efforts undertaken to ensure the credibility of carbon products to be traded through Singapore and to reduce Singapore's exposure to the risks of carbon trading.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry share an update of how this is progressing?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of the more than 20 countries that Singapore has begun exploring carbon credit agreements with, what is the portfolio of carbon projects the Government is focusing on to diversify and safeguard our carbon credit security?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What are the carbon offset criteria that companies can use to offset their carbon tax liabilities, and will the use of such carbon credits affect the amount of emissions that Singapore reports to the UNFCCC?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Industry advocates for the Government to consider prescribing an appropriate limit for ICC, or FPCC, that can be used to offset carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The industry feels that this 5% of taxable emission is rather insufficient.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A company with high abatement solution will achieve maximum 90% emission reduction limited by the existing technology.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For such a company, only 5% of the remaining 10% can be offset using carbon credit.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The third point is an implementation plan to the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Government plan to incentivise individuals to reduce our individual carbon footprint?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have to confess that I am still living in 24 degree celsius air-conditioning.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, in a post-Budget 2022 panel discussion, said, "It is with a combination of these different tools – taxes, incentives and standards – that Singapore can achieve its net-zero ambitions.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Moving early will, in fact, give Singapore a first-mover advantage to seize the opportunities that will arise from the new green economy." We would have all read in the news that during Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong's recent visit to Australia, Singapore signed a trailblazing Green Economy Agreement with Australia.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that several other jurisdictions are also exploring to do the same with us.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Carbon tax is the necessary price to pay in order to get serious decarbonisation actions and CO2 emission reduction underway.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, however, carbon tax is an evolving issue globally and we need to be able to be agile and adaptable, in order to respond to global trends.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, unwise to be over-prescriptive in our laws at this stage and it is also in my opinion unwise to have to share everything – all details and full disclosure.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I think we have to draw a line between being transparent and getting everyone to be accountable versus showing everything, because that is going to not be practical in the first place; and secondly, there is companies' competitiveness at stake.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am encouraged to see that a sensible, practical transition framework is built into the amendment Bill for allowances to balance our competitiveness, even as we green our way forward with the two sets of targeted policies, regulations, fiscal incentives and taxes, as is the subject of our debate today.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is imperative that we do not throw the baby out with the bath water.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our competitiveness cannot be taken for granted as our economy and jobs are dependent on our attractiveness as a location for investments.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Climate change is the crisis of the same scale as COVID-19, even as it is different.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For me, I would liken climate change to be as if we are the frog in the water in a pot over a slow, simmering flame.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It has been cooking for a long time and act together now we must, to jump out of that pot.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that Singapore can emerge very well just as we did from COVID-19 and just as our pioneers did after separation from Malaysia, because our people, our businesses and our Government work hand-in-hand in our unique tripartite relationship to seize the first-mover advantage to transition to a green economy.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed amendments to the CPA are a positive step in the right direction and I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I would, however, like to clarify the following points.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: One suggestion would be to allocate some of these to research and development (R&D) programmes related to green energy and sustainability, or education programmes to prepare companies for carbon tax reporting.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I recognise that there are opportunities for Singapore to pivot importing renewable energy from nearby countries; however, this would increase the reliance from overseas sources and affect our energy security.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, I would like to reiterate my firm support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It reinforces Singapore's commitment to a net-zero emissions country by 2050 and forces us to find solutions to demonstrate competitiveness in a low-carbon future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Just as we need a higher GST to help fund the healthcare needs of a population that is ageing surely and quickly with every passing day, we need a right price signal for carbon across the whole of our economy and our society, in a world that is heading quickly towards temperatures that are 1.5 to 2 degree celsius above pre-industrial levels, a world in which extreme weather has become more and more real for more and more people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Climate change is an existential threat, so we need the right price signal for carbon in Singapore urgently to drive the necessary changes in behaviour, by both individual consumers and businesses and producers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Three years on, there is an urgent need to do more, to ensure that "the price is right" – that the price signal for carbon is right.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet, this could not have come at a more challenging time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In what Senior Minister Tharman has described as a "perfect long storm", climate change is converging with other structural fragilities, like rising interest rates and inflation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the need to bear a higher but right cost of carbon – now – is competing with very real concerns about costs of living, concerns that are immediate and real.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Of course, in the medium term, by the end of a few years, we hope that individuals' consumption patterns would have changed and businesses would be well on their way to transit to low-carbon business models and practices, and the cost impact of carbon to both individuals and businesses and across the whole economy would have reached a new equilibrium, plateau, or even come down.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But there is no avoiding that we are raising carbon tax soon in the eye of this "perfect long storm" and a cost impact – higher costs – now and in the near term is almost unavoidable, coinciding with a period in which costs of living are sharply rising.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Electricity prices will go up because of the higher price of carbon.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Public transport costs will likely go up too.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I like to ask and seek clarification on how does the Government plan to help Singaporeans cope with and adjust to this new normal of low carbon?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Beyond the impact on costs of living, another very real concern of a higher carbon tax is the potential impact on Singapore's economic competitiveness, especially for traditionally emission-intensive trade-exposed industries.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How do we make sure we remain competitive in the region and that whole industries, like petrochemicals and electronics, do not lift and shift out of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How do we ensure that Singaporeans can continue to look forward to good jobs in these industries in a low-carbon future?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can the Government share more details about how it plans to work with industry to build new capabilities, and indeed, turn this strategic challenge into new and exciting opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, traditionally, emission-intensive industries can, and must, become a part of our future green economy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And while the competition may be regional, markets for these emission-intensive trade-exposed industries are, in fact, global.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And these markets will lead and define the demand for low-carbon products and services in the future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, we have an opportunity in Singapore to build future green capabilities for the world, position Singapore as a global hub to leapfrog the status quo and help the world produce green products and services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How might we better communicate this vision to all Singaporeans and make all of us part of this journey to turn the carbon constraint into exciting opportunities, and to turn the low-carbon challenge into a whole new world of possibilities in the next chapter of our Singapore Story, just as we have done for water, gas and land, in the Singapore Story thus far.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I would just like to ask if he has considered the impact of this proposal on both cost of living and economic competitiveness, as so many of our Members have raised.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: I like to thank the Member Mr Xie for his question.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: More importantly, I do recognise and agree with the Member's point in terms of supporting households in this transition and this is something which we have spoken about in the earlier debates as well.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This is a bold announcement, given Singapore's alternative energy disadvantaged position and our absolute dependence on the imported LNG for 95% of our country's electricity generation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, as a responsible member of the international community committed to fight the climate emergency, Singapore's strategic commitment to achieve net zero by 2050 is a necessary undertaking.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What does Singapore have to do differently in order to meet the net-zero goal?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the long term, we will have to scale-up the use of emerging technologies in low-carbon hydrogen, carbon capture utilisation and storage and maybe, light nuclear energy production.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the medium term, we will have to purchase clean electricity imports and step-up utilisation of solar energy, to progressively decarbonise the power sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In the short term, we will have to aggressively abate carbon emissions in our economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, the carbon tax is an important price signal and also an instrument to nudge industries, to internalise the cost of carbon emissions into their business costs and to adopt low-carbon business practices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Government is cognisant of the cost burden of the carbon tax on businesses and the consequential impact on cost of living that will be passed onto the consumers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, only facilities that produces more than 25,000 kilotonne CO2 emissions annually, will be subjected to the carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Even the long-term carbon tax of $50 to $80 expected in 2030, will still be considered comparable to the tax rates in other jurisdictions, for example in Europe, where carbon taxes can go beyond $100 per tonne CO2 emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In general, the business community here is appreciative that the introduction of carbon tax has been gradual, so that there is sufficient response time to prepare for this transition.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And I am heartened to learn from the Minister that the revenue collected from carbon taxes are not meant for the purposes of deriving additional Government revenue.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Instead, the collection will be ploughed back to support decarbonisation efforts and transition to a green economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, perhaps more could be done to enable this green transition, to help the industries and to achieve better decarbonisation results.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are the additional decarbonisation programmes, incentives and subsidies that would be implemented to help industries, especially SMEs and large local enterprises (LLEs), transit into the green economy?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What is the budget that is set aside for these programmes and incentives?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Together with the transport sector – which contributes 14% of carbon emissions – these are the three key sectors that account for almost all of Singapore's carbon emissions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Clearly, the increase in carbon taxes in 2023 will add greater cost pressures to industries that are already facing the triple whammy of the COVID-19 pandemic, higher energy costs and GST increase next year.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Hence, I agree that the transition framework is a prudent strategy to help the EITE sectors ride out this cost increase wave, so that they can remain competitive against rivals in other jurisdictions that have nil or lower carbon taxes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, it will require a fine balance and sound judgement to use the carbon tax as a stick for some industries while for other companies, the carbon tax can be waived to help them with transition.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As outlined in section 20D and 20E of the amended Bill, discretionary powers are vested with the Minister for Trade and Industry and appointed public bodies to assess each company's decarbonisation plans and determine if they are eligible for carbon tax exemption.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: On this note, may I ask the Minister if an impact analysis of carbon taxes on the overall business costs of affected companies has been carried out, in particular, for our SMEs and LLEs?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Also, how much transition time will companies in the EITE sectors be given before they are subjected to the full-blown effect of the carbon tax increase?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For companies outside the EITE sectors, given that Singapore's transition to cleaner green energy may only materialise well beyond 2030, how will companies, whose carbon emissions result mainly from the brownout electricity needed for their operations, be assisted in the next decade?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These companies may be paying both higher electricity tariffs due to the current energy crisis as well as increased carbon taxes for the carbon emissions generated.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, they may have to purchase renewable energies through private purchase agreements in order to meet carbon targets.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Does MTI know the number of companies that will be in such a predicament and how can they be assisted in the energy transition?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Also, as carbon emissions accounting and ESG standards are still not fully harmonised, are there adequate well-qualified consultants in the market to help companies, especially the SMEs and LLEs, to account for their carbon emissions footprint, to advise them on the sustainability strategies and to project the corresponding carbon taxes?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Will these consultants need to be accredited by the Ministry?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If so, will there be guidelines on consultancy fees chargeable to prevent companies from being subjected to paying yet another hefty layer of cost?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Minister can shed some light on these implementation considerations so that businesses and their sustainability officers can have a clearer idea as they plan for next year's financial budget and dedicate resources for their decarbonisation plans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Moreover, only high-quality ICCs that are compliant with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement under the UNFCCC and fulfill the ICAO CORSIA standards as the minimum standards, will be considered eligible for surrender.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I understand that the rationale is to set a high bar, so as to prevent greenwashing and also to ensure that industries prioritise carbon emissions reduction as the main pathway for decarbonisation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, there will be three issues to consider.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Should such high prices prevail, then ICCs would become irrelevant for businesses as an alternative to paying carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is well-placed to be a leading carbon services and trading hub.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's robust legislative framework and position as an established professional services, trading and financial hub, will put us in a good position to support the development of an internationally trusted carbon services and trading ecosystem in Asia.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Thirdly, there are currently only two international exchanges in Singapore trading voluntary carbon credits, namely AirCarbon Exchange (ACX), established in 2019, and Climate Impact X (CIX), established in May 2021.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The primary concern is that carbon credits are still not sufficiently reliable in quality because of multiple certification standards and processes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How will the ICC framework help these carbon credit exchanges ensure that the quality and consistency of carbon credits traded comply with global standards?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How will the ICC help to further develop the domestic carbon credits market?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To this end, I hope the Minister will clarify the impact of the ICC framework on the future of carbon credit exchanges and our plans to develop Singapore as a leading carbon services and trading hub.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, the long-term energy strategy to reach net-zero goals will be much more challenging.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Alongside the revised NDC to achieve net zero by 2050, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also announced the National Hydrogen Strategy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: A lot of effort and resources will be needed for research and technology, as well as for new storage and distribution infrastructure, amongst others.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Unfortunately, Singapore just does not have sufficient renewable energy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: That way, the carbon taxes collected will play a meaningful role to help Singapore achieve a much more sustainable and a secured energy solution portfolio that is needed to achieve net-zero emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Earlier, Minister Grace Fu has highlighted the urgent need for the world to address climate change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Singapore is firmly committed to doing our part in the global effort to reduce GHGs emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And to meet our climate commitments, we have put in place a robust suite of measures to spur and support our companies to decarbonise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As climate action gains greater urgency globally, the transition towards lower carbon and carbon neutral operations will increasingly become a pre-requisite for consumers, for investors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Hence, it is in the company's commercial interest to decarbonise and, in the same way, it is also critical for Singapore to transit to a low-carbon economy to maintain our long-term economic competitiveness, to remain an attractive investment and business destination as reminded by Ms Janet Ang, Mr Xie Yao Quan and many other Members during their very passionate speeches earlier, and to ensure good jobs for Singaporeans and good jobs created here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have sought public and the industry feedback on the draft Carbon Pricing (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The majority of the respondents acknowledged the role of an appropriate price signal for carbon in order to enable the low-carbon transition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, some respondents will favour a more aggressive carbon tax trajectory, given the latest recommendations by the IPCC for stronger actions to reach the Paris Agreement goals and the urgency to reduce rising greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: On the other hand, some companies are concerned that the higher carbon tax will add to cost pressures, especially for the export-oriented companies that have to compete with those from jurisdictions with lower or no effective carbon price.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Apart from the public consultation and since the announcement of the changes to carbon tax earlier this year, we have been engaging businesses that will be directly impacted by the increase.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We appreciate their feedback that they recognise the need for an appropriate carbon price, but they are also concerned about the impact of higher carbon taxes on their operating costs and competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We hear and we understand their need for time to make the necessary investments and changes to transit towards greener operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is especially so for companies that depend on low-carbon technologies which are still under development, such as CCUS, like low-carbon hydrogen that some of the Members talked about – Ms Poh Li San, Mr Cheng Hsing Yao and Mr Xie Yao Quan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I want to assure the House that in designing the carbon tax framework, we have taken into consideration all these varying views and feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And I want to assure the House that we will continue engaging companies on their sustainability journey, including our SMEs and LLEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Businesses that are large emitters, for example in the energy and chemical sectors, will be directly impacted by the carbon tax.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We recognise the challenges that companies face, especially amid other increasingly tough operating conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The impact of the revised carbon tax regime will be especially pronounced for companies in the EITE sectors, such as the chemicals as well as the semiconductor sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Ms Janet Ang, and also Mr Xie Yao Quan – during their speeches, reminded us that these companies compete globally and face competition from counterparts in jurisdictions which have lower or, in fact, no carbon prices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In addition, many jurisdictions with carbon prices offer generous allowances and support to companies in EITE sectors to protect their business competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The allowances provided could cover as high as 100% of the companies' emissions in some of these countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This demonstrates our commitment to work closely with the industries to make the green transition as smooth as possible and by providing companies with advance notice, we hope it will facilitate their business decisions and plans for decarbonisation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: During her passionate speech, Ms Janet Ang reminded us that many EITE companies have placed significant and substantial investments in Singapore that continue to provide good jobs and secured jobs for Singaporeans and contribute to our economic growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Members Mr Don Wee and Mr Leon Perera have asked if the transition framework will erode the price signal for companies to decarbonise and if the framework should be tightened.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Singapore has committed to enhancing our 2030 NDCs to reduce our emissions to around 60 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2030 and that is after peaking emissions earlier and to achieve net zero by year 2050.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This means that the Singapore Government is accountable to these international climate commitments, and hence, we will ensure that the transition framework will effectively, robustly drive companies to decarbonise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To address Mr Don Wee's concern, we will work with companies, including the large emitters, to ensure they have decarbonisation plans aligned with Singapore's net-zero commitment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This will be determined based on internationally recognised efficiency benchmarks where available or based on the facilities' decarbonisation plans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This means that any emissions above the allowances will still be taxed at the prevailing carbon tax rate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In time, when appropriate, the Government will also release aggregated information on the number of allowances provided, but I think Members have also raised, and they understand, that we will need to bear in mind considerations, such as whether such disclosures inadvertently divulge commercially sensitive information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In addition, the allowances will also be reviewed regularly against how the companies have fared against the efficiency benchmarks where available or based on their decarbonisation plans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Earlier in their speeches, Mr Cheng Hsing Yao and Ms Janet Ang spoke about the need to ensure that we are not being too prescriptive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We need to ensure that the framework retains some flexibility, adaptability to ensure that as we transit into a low-carbon future, Singapore remains a compelling and attractive business and investment location here, so that we can create good jobs, including new green jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will also take into consideration international developments as well as technological developments of decarbonisation technologies, including CCUS, low-carbon hydrogen, much like how Ms Janet Ang spoke about the need to consider the state of technology development in determining the allowances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, I can assure her that we will keep our eyes and ears very close on the global development, not just the efficiency standards, but also low-carbon technology developments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Many of these investments were made amidst a different operating context and would require time for them to transit, for them to make the necessary investment to ease into lower carbon operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Without transitory support, there will be a significant near-term impact on their competitiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, the transitionary support would especially help companies that have made large capital investments in Singapore, and have contributed to our economic story and the growth of jobs here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Members reminded us that today, as we debate this Bill, Singapore is the only country within Southeast Asia to implement a carbon price regime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, we want to make sure we mitigate any risks of carbon leakage because such an outcome would actually lead to loss of jobs and loss of economic value in Singapore, with no overall global reduction in emissions, if there is carbon leakage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Louis Ng, in his earlier speech, and Ms Poh Li San asked about the period of transition that will be provided to companies in the EITE sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I want to assure them that we will calibrate the duration of the transition framework based on international standards, developments and technological developments or decarbonisation techniques.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are aware that the carbon prices in other jurisdictions are not static – some may continue to maintain very low and, in some cases, no carbon prices for certain sectors at all, while others may raise carbon prices more aggressively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are keeping a very close eye on that.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We also recognise that companies will need time to transition to low-carbon operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Government will consider all these factors when calibrating the transition framework.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will also inform companies in advance of the changes to facilitate business planning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Leon Perera earlier proposed that the allowances be awarded only to facilities that have received allowances for no more than one of the four preceding emissions' years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I want to share with him that companies had shared with us during the consultation that they need time to develop and implement new technologies to decarbonise and transform their operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This effort could take a couple of years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Hence, restricting allowances in the manner suggested will not provide the support that is needed by the companies, nor meet the intended objective of the transition framework.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Leon Perera also proposed that the awards of allowances, includes information such as reasons for awarding the allowances, be listed on a public registry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Earlier on, Ms Janet Ang shared that doing this might be unwise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Members will appreciate that doing so may reveal commercially sensitive information about a facility's scale of operations, revenue and so on, and over time really erode Singapore's competitiveness as a business and investment location and then at the end of the day, it will affect our ability to create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Earlier, I said that the Government will, in time, release aggregated information on the amount of allowances provided.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I have also explained the reasons and the basis for awarding the allowances earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Don Wee earlier also asked if Singapore is considering a Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Having said that, we will continue to monitor the global developments on CBAM and calibrate our position accordingly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao and Mr Mark Chay spoke about the need to ensure energy security, resilience and to preserve optionality as Singapore moves towards our net-zero emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I fully agree with them because energy security is always at the top of our minds even as we seek to decarbonise our grid.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, as we scale up electricity imports, we will put in place sufficient backup generation capacity to ensure a continuous supply, even in the event of disruptions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Many Members also spoke about how we recently announced our National Hydrogen Strategy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Indeed, like what Mr Cheng Hsing Yao, Ms Poh Li San and other Members have said, hydrogen can complement and diversify our power mix alongside with solar, alongside with imported electricity as well as other potential low-carbon energy sources.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In importing hydrogen, like other energy sources, we will adopt a diversified portfolio to ensure energy security and to ensure energy resilience.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We are pressing ahead with the development of such low-carbon alternatives, which will provide more options for businesses and consumers seeking to purchase renewable energy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: But even so, and especially in the interim, I think Members will agree with us that both businesses and consumers – and in fact – all of us must play a part and improve energy efficiency and optimise and reduce energy consumption.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Ms Poh Li San, Mr Xie Yao Quan, Ms Janet Ang and Mr Mark Chay asked about the support for companies that are paying higher electricity prices either due to the current energy situation, or indirectly, due to the carbon tax.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We understand the challenges that our businesses are facing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We recognise that the companies will be affected by the indirect impact of the carbon tax, through electricity prices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Earlier on, Second Minister Tan See Leng addressed many of these energy Parliamentary Questions and shared with the House that as Singapore imports more than 90% of our energy needs, we cannot be fully insulated from developments, including volatilities in the global energy market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is why we have adopted a calibrated approach of right-pricing electricity to help encourage prudent use of electricity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: At the same time, we will continue to support our businesses and SMEs to make more sustainable business decisions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is equivalent to an abatement of over 1,700 tonnes of carbon emissions annually.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is one REG(E) project and we want to encourage our companies to come on board the various schemes, whether it is the REG(E) or E2F, or the more recently rolled out Energy Efficiency Grant (EEG).

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To Mr Mark Chay's query, we also periodically review these schemes to assess if updates and refinements are needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We want to make sure they are relevant and accessible to our SMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: NEA has also recently simplified the grant application as well as the disbursement process for the standard retrofit projects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, this makes it easier for SMEs and companies to apply and to benefit from the E2F.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This example is of a local company that has benefited from the E2F.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The company's name is Kawarin Enterprise Pte Ltd.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With the support from the Energy Efficiency Fund, Kawarin upgraded their old air compressors to more energy-efficient models.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This has allowed Kawarin Enterprise Pte Ltd to enjoy annual cost savings of more than S$30,000 and abated about 48 tonnes of carbon annually.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, I hope that Members of the House will help us to share this information and allow more SMEs and local companies to benefit from all this array of programmes that we have availed to them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: I want to assure the House that the Government will continue to monitor overall costs for businesses, which could be driven by many factors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We have discussed about that besides the carbon tax, and MTI and the economic agencies stand ready to provide more assistance when needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Because by working in partnership and taking the necessary bold steps today, we can chart Singapore's transformation towards a greener and more sustainable future together.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I am heartened that all Members agree that the revised carbon tax regime set out in the Bill is a decisive step in climate action.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They have been calibrated to enable the pace of transformation needed to achieve our net-zero ambition, while allowing businesses to stay economically competitive as they embark on their low-carbon transition.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our approach provides certainty by giving advance notice to companies and announcing the rates ahead of time.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I will respond to Members' questions on the issues raised, under three broad themes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: How do we maintain a strong impetus, ensuring that the allowances granted under the transition framework do not blunt the purpose of the carbon price and that the ICC regime is robust?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Minister of State Low Yen Ling has addressed Members' questions on the transition framework and industry support schemes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I will speak about the ICC regime shortly.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members spoke on the need to maintain our economic competitiveness amidst the transition to a low-carbon economy, which Minister of State Low Yen Ling has spoken on.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Many Members have also highlighted how this new carbon tax regime can create new growth opportunities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: How can we support a vibrant carbon services ecosystem in Singapore which can create good, green jobs for Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As we update the carbon tax regime, how do we deliver an inclusive transition towards a low-carbon society?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Ms Janet Ang has highlighted, we must ensure that the carbon credits surrendered, or "offset", are of high environmental integrity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms He Ting Ru brought up the same point.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: CORSIA standards are amongst the most rigorous in carbon markets worldwide and they include criteria, such as additionality and permanence – issues that Ms He Ting Ru has mentioned. "Additionality" means that emission reductions must be "above business as usual" levels.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Permanence requires emission reductions to be durable and irreversible.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Furthermore, we will ensure alignment with international rules, such as Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Double counting occurs when an eligible ICC accrues to both Singapore and the host country producing this ICC.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To prevent this ICC from being double counted, the host country must authorise a corresponding adjustment, to "give up" the emissions reduction to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This will provide more clarity to companies and to the public on what our eligibility criteria entail.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: By placing emphasis on the quality of eligible ICC surrendered, we ensure that companies exercise care and due diligence in sourcing high-quality ICC responsibly and avoid the associated pitfalls, as Ms Janet Ang and Ms He Ting Ru have highlighted.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: When ready, the registry will serve as a record-keeping system to track and account for the usage of ICC by carbon tax-liable companies to offset their taxable emissions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The ICC registry will be an integral part of our ICC framework.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In developing and implementing our ICC framework, we have been and will continue to work closely with industry players, green groups and other key stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There is also a parallel work stream that is going on on the voluntary market side.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, MAS, the Singapore Exchange (SGX), for example, are hard at work to contribute to credible and robust taxonomies.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is a very nascent area and I think many parties, many different organisations, different sectors, are working very quickly to get alignment and harmonisation of standards.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Singapore must be there in order to have the first-mover advantage that Ms Janet Ang has talked about.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In this way, we hope that by having the ICC as a foundation, the voluntary markets can take guidance and also benefit from the carbon services competencies that we will help develop in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, although this Bill does not address the voluntary carbon market, which I will talk about later on, I hope that my explanation on what we are doing on ICC will help address some of the concerns over greenwashing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, on the economy and creating growth opportunities, specifically, how the Government will unlock supply of ICC and support the growth of the carbon services and trading ecosystem in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I agree with Ms Janet Ang on the importance of diversifying our sources of credit supply, including our source countries and the types of carbon credit projects.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I spoke earlier about our Government-to-Government engagements, which are progressing well.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will advance talks with like-minded countries to establish implementation agreements and bilateral frameworks to guide interested parties to procure and trade in high-quality credits.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: At the technical level, we are working closely with key players in the carbon services and trading ecosystem to develop the ICC framework.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our intent is for the ICC framework to catalyse local demand in carbon markets and support our vision of establishing Singapore as a carbon services and trading hub.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Carbon services are a promising potential growth area for Singapore that can create good, green jobs for Singaporeans, while contributing to the global agenda on climate change.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Growth in carbon markets will drive demand for jobs related to low-carbon project development, financing, consultancy and measurement, reporting and verification, or MRV.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: One notable example is the Climate Action Data Trust, or CAD Trust, which will be officially launched next month as a global market infrastructure supported by the World Bank, the International Emissions Trading Association and the Singapore Government.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The CAD Trust will be anchored in Singapore to provide an open-source system to link and harmonise information about carbon credits and projects across registries globally.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This initiative will drive market transparency, strengthen trust and advance global climate action.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And Singapore, I think, is well-placed because we have developed trust and confidence with investors over decades, and we will maintain this confidence and high-level integrity in this new area that we go into as well.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The CAD Trust will join a thriving ecosystem of over 70 organisations in Singapore, providing carbon services to the region and beyond.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Janet Ang asked if the Government plans to ensure the credibility of voluntary carbon trading activities in Singapore and manage related risks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Other Members also asked about the development of voluntary carbon trading activities.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is not envisaged for this Bill to address that.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our approach is to build up a vibrant carbon services ecosystem and provide the space for leading international and corporate initiatives to shape the voluntary marketplace.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These include the Voluntary Carbon Markets Integrity Initiative and the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market, which develop guidelines that promote the trading of voluntary carbon credits with high environmental integrity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As companies' use of voluntary carbon credits evolves, we will continue to study whether there is a need to adopt a more prescriptive approach.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Poh Li San and Ms Janet Ang raised concerns that setting the facility-level limit for the use of ICCs at 5% might be too low, considering the current limitations in technologies that can achieve emissions reduction at scale and the need to support a vibrant carbon market.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, what we will do is to start at 5% as the limit that we think that we can manage and then, as the market develops, we will see how it goes and we will make changes along the way.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, I would just like to say to Members that in this phase, let us not be too prescriptive.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Let us have an effective system that can help us grow from a very nascent stage to something that we can be proud of.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This brings me to Ms He Ting Ru's proposed amendment pertaining to instances where the prescribed facility-level limit is lifted.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are not able to support this proposed amendment, as it involves the publication of identifiable information relating to the registered business facility and breaches the confidentiality of carbon tax data which companies are accorded under the CPA.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I hope that I have explained sufficiently how our overall framework supports transactions of high environmental standards and that there are sufficient safeguards in terms of the registry, in terms of standards that will allow a nascent system to grow.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I understand that Ms He Ting Ru has suggested that perhaps we can have disclosure without financial details.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But imagine if we are in a situation where we are discussing with companies on what type of ICC they are going to engage in and if a company has something that is groundbreaking, that requires significant ICC to justify the investment, but the system up there says that "Look, anything above 5% – disclosure, disclosure – even though details are not there, your names will be flashed on the papers".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Do you think there will be more companies stepping forward or there will be fewer companies stepping forward?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, we have to be quite practical at this stage, feel our way through and then, if we find that 5% is, indeed, not sufficient, Members can be assured that I will come back to this Chamber to ask for this level to be increased because we are all in the same boat, we want the same thing, which is a well-functioning carbon credit system that has environmental integrity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I will now address the final group of issues which deal with balancing the interests of all stakeholders as we manage a fair and inclusive transition.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Janet Ang and Mr Louis Ng asked about the Government's plan for the carbon tax to be imposed on more emitters, beyond the large emitters.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Coupled with our existing taxes on transport fuels, which are not subjected to carbon tax – we have separate taxes on fuels – we are achieving around 90% coverage.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how compliance costs would increase if the next tier of facilities – that is, the reportable facilities – were taxed as well.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Such facilities would have to incur not just the cost of reporting or the cost of paying taxes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They will have to get their reported emissions verified because, once you have to pay tax, we will need you to have it checked by experts, by auditors, and this will be a cost burden for a company, perhaps with a much lower carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, it will be disproportionate to the carbon tax payable.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Public disclosure of data needs to be contextualised, so that it can be interpreted fairly and meaningfully.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our large emitters have products and production processes that are often heterogenous, specialised and proprietary.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Publishing the emissions or ranking of top emitters without providing context of the business and the nature or the size of its operation may not be helpful in understanding how well a company is doing in mitigating its emissions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Two refineries, same products altogether, both getting the same kind of allowances, is that definitely fair?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: What if I tell you that one refinery is actually adopting very, very carbon-inefficient processes, the other one is way ahead?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Without background information, without understanding its processes, you cannot just look at two numbers and say, "This is fair" or "this is not fair" and "Why are you all giving this?" There must be a workable system and I think, as Minister of State Low Yen Ling has explained, companies have to be benchmarked, they will have to produce their decarbonisation plans so that we can support them on a multi-year decarbonisation journey.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For accountability to their stakeholders, we encourage all companies to size, analyse and publish their environmental impact to explain how they are managing emissions-related risks, in relation to their commitment to decarbonisation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Companies listed locally are already subjected to SGX requirements to do so, as in many jurisdictions globally.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Nonetheless, we will study possible ways to better facilitate environmental impact disclosure in a manner that respects commercial sensitivity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We appreciate the concerns from Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Xie Yao Quan, Mr Mark Chay and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim that the revised carbon tax levels will lead to higher costs amidst rising inflationary pressures.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members of both sides of the House recognise that the effectiveness of a carbon tax to drive decarbonisation depends on the price level and have spoken in support of a raise in the carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We all agree that $5 is not right.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And global warming does not pause because of inflation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
