text: So, rather than holding back our plans, the Government has been and will continue to provide support in a targeted manner to affected businesses and households as part of our longstanding commitment to an inclusive low-carbon transition.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And this is where I listened very carefully to Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, and I have difficulty accepting his recommendations on implementation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, he has acknowledged that he has actually asked for a higher carbon tax range.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, I am glad that the Workers' Party is supporting an even higher carbon tax range.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, you are my best champion along with me.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim went on to say that this is not a very good time, like many of the Members as well, because we have inflation, we have energy shortages.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, perhaps, instead of giving a fixed number that may bind the hands of policymakers of the future, he has suggested that the carbon tax adhere to a central rate but with a variable component that varies over time according to conditions of the economy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In other hands, scale back when the economy is in recession, raise when the economy is strong.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As much as Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has suggested this as a way to ease implementation, I would find it hard to implement.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First of all, I would like Assoc Prof Jamus Lim to give me a three-year projection of what the economic conditions will be and then what that variation would be.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have all seen how exogenous factors have affected our economic conditions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We go out to the market, stand in the Chamber here and say, "By the way, we are going to raise carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It is somewhere around $80 to $133 per tonne.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But, you know, there is some middle number and then you can move around a bit." How can companies make plans like that?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: When you want them to invest in a plant that is energy-efficient, that captures carbon or uses green hydrogen, you have to tell them what is likely going to be the prevailing carbon tax so that when they do a multi-year calculation, as Member Leon Perera has stated that is what companies would do, sometimes even up to 10, 20 years, they need to have certainty.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Otherwise, they will not be able to price in the effect of a higher carbon price.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Otherwise, it will be unfair to companies who have invested in hydrogen and then turn around and find that there are no takers because the carbon price differential is missing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The Government said that it was going to do it, but because of the economic situation, is now not doing.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, we find it very hard to accept his suggestion.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, if you are going to push back one, two years until the recession is completely over – which I really do not know when that is going to be – that means that it leaves us with about four years to raise it from $5 to $100 per tonne.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, with humility, I would say that I find it hard to accept his suggestion for implementation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Poh Li San and Mr Don Wee have pointed out that the Government does not expect to derive additional revenue from the upcoming revisions to the carbon tax and that is correct.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The carbon tax revenue will be used to accelerate decarbonisation efforts and Singapore's inclusive transition to a green economy.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Minister of State Low Yen Ling has spoken about how the Government is supporting our industry along their decarbonisation journey, In addition to energy efficiency support measures for businesses, Mr Mark Chay will be pleased to note that we have earmarked funds under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 (RIE2025) plan for the research, development and demonstration of low-carbon technologies that can drive deeper decarbonisation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will cushion the impact on our households.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, while I cannot accept Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's suggestion, we will have to, from time to time, evaluate our carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Maybe we have it too high, maybe we have it too low, maybe we can move faster, maybe there are already technologies out there that can make carbon capture cost-effective.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will have to change, but we need to give companies sufficient notice.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And in a year when business is bad, or utilities' costs are high like what we are experiencing now, you can be assured that the Government will have very targeted measures that are relevant for that time and the same with households.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have not even raised carbon tax yet.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, none of the higher utilities costs today is attributable to carbon tax – it is only to come in 2024.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: When the carbon tax was first introduced in 2019, U-Save rebates were provided to offer transitional support to help affected households adjust.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have been and will continue to support households with U-Save rebates.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Members would know, I think in the last six to 12 months, we have been supporting our households because of inflation, because of higher utilities costs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And it is no secret that we support households in 4-room flats for up to five months of utilities bills.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And just to put things into context again, carbon tax as it stands now, for a year, every year, we are collecting to the grand tune of $200 million.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, it is not enough to affect the costs of goods.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is to give you a measure of the scale that we are talking about.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are prepared to support households even way above what we are collecting, whether it is GST or whether it is carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Members have the assurance that while we have fixed the carbon tax according to a schedule to give companies certainty, we will always be mindful about the needs of companies, the needs of households, the needs of society when the increase is implemented.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are also reviewing ongoing schemes, such as the Climate Friendly Households Programme, to encourage more households to mitigate the long-term cost impact by making the switch to energy-efficient appliances and water-saving fittings.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, if Members have residents who fit the criteria who want to reduce their utilities bills by switching to more energy-efficient appliances, please step forward, please ask them to apply to NEA.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Since then, we have accelerated our sustainability journey and stepped up our climate ambition.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Ms Poh Li San noted, achieving net zero by 2050 will be a daunting, but necessary undertaking.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With our enhanced climate targets, our carbon pricing regime must evolve in tandem.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As Members have noted in today's debate, our carbon tax regime must strike a fine balance between three imperatives: the environment, our economy and our society.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To reach our ambition of net-zero emissions by 2050, we must drive decarbonisation while ensuring that ICCs are sourced from projects of high environmental integrity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And here again, I would like to thank all Members who have spoken in support of a higher carbon tax rate, and particularly, I note Workers' Party's position.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: All Workers' Party Members – Ms He Ting Ru, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, Mr Leon Perera and Mr Louis Chua – supported the need for carbon tax and want an even higher carbon tax.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: They think that we are still too low at $50 to $80 per tonne.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, I would really want to raise it as high as possible.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, I would say that you really are along with me on this journey.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We must strive to deliver an inclusive transition for our society, spur action across the whole of society and catalyse partnerships across the people, public and private sectors.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Taken together, they will enable the next lap of our green transition and lay the building blocks for Singapore as an economically competitive global sustainability hub.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: With an effective carbon price as the cornerstone of our climate mitigation efforts, the Government will continue to push the envelope on all fronts, to secure a climate resilient and sustainable future for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I call on all Members of the House to give your support to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And, like the Minister, I would also emphasise that there is agreement from Members of both the ruling party and the Opposition on the need for us to hike the carbon price and on the broad thrusts of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just have a few clarifications on the points that the Minister mentioned in relation to some of the amendments that we have filed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Were that to happen, were that possibility to be left open in the legislation, that possibility would undermine wider public acceptance of a much-needed carbon price hike, and perhaps, acceptance within the business community itself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The second clarification is, would the Government acknowledge that, notwithstanding the changes that we have suggested to the allowance regime, the Government possesses other tools through other laws, other powers that allow it to apply economic incentives in cases where it may really be necessary to prevent disinvestment for job creation, job defence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And that would allow us to have a carbon pricing regime where the curtailment on the allowance regime is a bit clearer and the transparency level is a bit better, but at the same time, we are still able to retain and win these strategically important projects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My third clarification is, in terms of the public registry that we have suggested.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would the Government acknowledge that there are some benefits to that transparency?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And my last clarification is, if the Government does not wish to have this public register, I believe both Minister of State Low Yen Ling and Minister Grace Fu referred to the Government is studying, publishing some kind of aggregate data in the future.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I want to assure him, and also the House, that even as we put in place the transition framework to support the EITE companies to transit to low-carbon future, I want to assure him that we maintain the impetus for them to decarbonise as quickly as possible.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In fact, we want to catalyse the process for them to do so.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And certainly, as we roll out the transition framework, it will not give any companies a free pass.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And Members said that, as far as Singapore is concerned, people know that when we say we will do it, we will achieve it.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: In fact, we will put in place interim milestones to make sure we get there by 2030 and by 2050.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And so, the Singapore Government is certainly accountable to this international climate commitment.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: That is why the transition framework that we put in place is meant to ensure that the EITE companies are able to catalyse their decarbonisation journey.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: All these plans, I can assure you, will be scrutinised and there will be checks and balances within the relevant authority and within the Ministry, and in fact, across Ministries, because as far as climate change is concerned, we have an Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change (IMCCC).

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, there are checks and balances, there is accountability, there is transparency.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: I shared with the House earlier in my speech, in time, where appropriate, the Government will certainly release aggregated information on the amount of allowances provided.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: But I urge everyone to have a care.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: And I think Ms Janet Ang and many Members reminded us that at this very nascent stage, as we are creating this, to make sure that we are well-placed to capture the green opportunities, not just for SMEs, but also for Singaporean workers, our youths, our mid-career hires, and so on.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: We want to make sure that we do not overly constrain our ability to respond to the emerging market opportunities and the trends as well.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, we need to bear in mind whether such disclosures may inadvertently divulge commercially sensitive information now.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: Not just that, not just economic value-add, not just jobs, but they also form an important ecosystem for our local SMEs as their suppliers, as their business partners.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: So, these are really what is at stake.

speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
text: To make sure that we take a very calibrated approach as we put in place a transition framework, as we catalyse their transition to a low-carbon future, we want to make sure that we do not inadvertently diminish our competitiveness as a business and investment location, thereby hurting our ability to create good jobs for people in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We are an accountable Government and we are prepared to be accountable to the people.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, you are going to look at our commitments in 2030, our year-to-year carbon emissions and hold us accountable.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I think the line of questioning that the Member has taken, seems to suggest that we have something to hide and we need to hide some incentives somewhere else.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ultimately, you look at our Budget, every year – have we overspent?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Do we have items that are not accounted for?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Do we have schemes that cannot be explained to people?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I think our track record speaks for itself.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will stand in this House again, year after year, to justify to you how we have been doing on our Green Plan and our carbon emissions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first has to do with the notion of whether we are indeed calling for a higher rate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And the median I suggested was $100 a tonne.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is true, certainly, that in the long run, we seek for something of that nature for good reason, as I had explained.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It was the mid-point of what is scientifically credible and defensible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That said, I think it is important to distinguish between the appropriate level versus the manner by which we get to that level – the glide path, if you will.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The analogy is to think about how one might choose to target one's weight loss journey.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Let us say, I really wish to be 65 kilogrammes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, what is your clarification?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yes, so, the clarification then is whether the Ministry sees or does not see the merits of separating these two decisions – about the appropriate level of the carbon tax versus the glide path to get there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My second clarification has to do with something that she said about how businesses cannot operate without certainty, when we do not know what the carbon tax is going to be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Even now, the Government routinely alters levers of policy such as the interest rate when there is uncertainty on a year-to-year basis, about the level of interest rates, yet businesses continue to invest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Put it another way, let us say the Ministry telegraphed that it was originally going for —

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, originally the Ministry telegraphed the $25 a tonne rate next year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Would she believe that businesses would then be very upset if we said that we would scale this $25 a tonne back to something lower, to eventually raise it subsequently?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, I would like to maybe ask him for his suggestion of how the Government should be positioning the carbon tax in his way.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: What will be the target – it is $100, so, if it is long run, which year?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just to be clear, the Government has not also committed to a $50 a tonne —

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It was well stated: $58 to $133, with the mid-point being $100.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, your range is higher than the Government, is it correct?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The lower bound is lower than the Government's upper bound.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yes, the lower bound that I gave you is lower than the Government's upper bound.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Can you please try to tell me, if you are the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment, how would you glide to this number?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: You are going to go out and say, "Company, this is the new glide path." How would you describe your glide path?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I suggested that we could do it incrementally, the way that the Ministry has suggested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But I also suggested that we could allow the specific level to adjust upward and downward, according to economic conditions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, are you then saying that we can go out to the world, and say, "Sorry, I have made the 2030 NDC on the basis of certain economic conditions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And now that the economic conditions are bad, there is a war out there, there is high inflation in energy costs, my NDCs do not count because I need to glide further out"?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: No, but I think I was clear that the adjustments upwards and downwards are the same way that business cycles go upward and downward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, you would have it lower in a given year, because of economic conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But when things pick up, you would raise it back so that you met the original targets.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, you are suggesting a very variable carbon tax rate, ends with $58 to $133, but without knowing how it is going to get there.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Not even knowing what 2024 is going to be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I think you would set a target, but be able to adapt to economic conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The same way the interest rates are —

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Say, start with $25, as I said in my speech.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Okay, so in 2025, are you going to stay with $25 as well?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We would have to look at economic conditions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand that when a Member asks a question, the other Member sits down; question is answered, vice versa.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Can you please tell me, describe to me your carbon tax glide path in numbers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Because I am a business, I need to know.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Can you please tell me, with some certainty, what is that variable portion – even if you say $25 for two years to come, $45 I am not too sure, but what will be the variation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But I am pushing for the flexibility to adjust it upward or downward just to take into account of the fact that economic conditions may alter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The same way we do for interest rates.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This is a policy to change our energy mix and our energy use.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, whether there is going to be an economic downturn or not, this is a change that we all need to make.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And Members have spoken so passionately about the need to address the tragedy of the commons, climate change that is confronting us.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, are we going to delay it further?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The answer is we all need to change.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If there is an economic problem, if there is an interest rate problem, of course we have to deal with it.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have to deal with it in other ways.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But the signal to the companies must be that this is a path that the Government is going ahead with.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will have to make investments with these numbers in mind, bearing in mind that our investments in the petrochemical industry or in the power generation industry are multi-year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, if we have targets, carbon tax rates that cannot be even certain for the next four, five, six years, how can they make long-term projections?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I find it very difficult for companies to do that, I find it very difficult for financiers, for banks to also do that.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And here, I think I am receiving slightly mixed messages.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The message is, "We want to fly the environmental flag.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We want to be able to address our constituents who want us to be as green as possible".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But when it comes to the hard decision of making changes, of making companies change and invest in renewables, reduce efficiency, reduce utilities, reduce water, circular economy, reduce waste – "Hang on, I think there is an economic condition and, therefore, we change".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Is the carbon tax something that we need to do and if we need to do it, do we need certainty?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If we need certainty, how do we address conditions that we do not foresee?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If we have a COVID-19 again – touch wood, hope that we will never have it – but if we have a COVID-19, or we have a major recession; of course, we will have to think about ways to cushion it.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But that does not mean that we are turning back to fossil again.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: That is the message that we have been telling all the large emitters in the world at COP27.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Even though there is an energy crisis out there, please do not turn your eyes away from the problem.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, I hope that Members will support what we are doing, understand that we are not blind to concerns, accept that we need to give clarity to companies to invest, to change, to adopt a way of low-carbon production that we cannot delay anymore, even as we are confronting some major challenges out there.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: If I am not wrong, the Minister said earlier that our proposed registry would breach confidentiality protections afforded under the carbon pricing regime.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Or was she saying that there is a risk of some deduction being made to allow people to make inferences, bearing in mind again that we are not asking for details about the amount surrendered in excess of the 5%, which is the currently proposed threshold?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: And if she is saying that the Government is unable to support the registry, what safeguards are there to make sure that there is better accountability for the ICCs surrender regime?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: It is important for us to get this balance right, so that it does not end up making it look like entities can buy their way out of the decarbonisation process, even when that really is not the case under the regime?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
text: Also, just to follow on from my colleague, Mr Perera's point earlier, can we have a bit more details about what aggregate data will be published to address concerns that were previously mentioned?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Hold us accountable eventually for our overall performance on carbon abatement and carbon mitigation, but let us run an effective, flexible, nimble system, so that we can really catch the wind and be as effective as we can in developing a new green economy.

speaker: The Chairman
text: There are 12 amendments standing in the name of Mr Leon Perera, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The Minister for Finance has signified that the President's recommendation under Article 59(2) of the Constitution is required for amendments (1) to (3)* and (8) to (12)**.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Do these amendments have the recommendation of the President?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Perera, please proceed to move these amendments together.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And is it correct to say that the advice of the President was sought, but at the same time, the advice could only be given from the Office of the President based on the advice of the relevant Minister or the advice of the Cabinet?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, the specific amendments in question that Mr Leon Perera has asked me about, are the amendments in his Notice of Amendments, for clause 13, amendments (1) to (3) and amendments (8) to (12), in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Those financial matters would include, for example, increasing or reducing taxes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When a Bill has such fiscal implications, or when an amendment to a Bill has such fiscal implications, the President's recommendation is required.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is provided for under Standing Order 67(1), which provides that it is the duty of the Minister for Finance to inform the Speaker before moving amendments to a Bill, whether the recommendation of the President is required by law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It was done by way of notification to Parliament, which was circulated by way of Notice Paper No 1522 to all Members.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Which means that all Members, including Mr Leon Perera and the Workers' Party would be aware that the President's recommendation is necessary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Just in terms of timing, though, I need to remind Members that the Notice of Amendments actually came in two clear days before the Sitting, which means on Wednesday.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And that means, on Thursday and Friday, the Government had to look at the amendments and assess to see whether or not such amendments had any fiscal implications.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It was not, I should add, notified to us by the Workers' Party, who had prepared the amendments, that it would have fiscal implications – which one would actually expect you to do, knowing that the President's recommendation is to be signified.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we had to check that through and that took some time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Then, Mr Leon Perera's next question really is whether the President's recommendation was sought, and if so, when and so on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is because the Government has assessed that the amendments in question – that is amendments (1) to (3) and (8) to (12) – could not be supported on the merits.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We determined that they could not be supported for the reasons explained earlier by my colleagues, in the Second Reading debate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is a long-established feature of Westminster parliaments that the government of the day has the sole right and responsibility to initiate financial legislation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government may, therefore, also take the decision not to put forward amendments with financial implications for the recommendation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, can I just give a brief response to Minister Indranee Rajah's points on procedure?

speaker: The Chairman
text: We are not having a debate on this issue.

speaker: The Chairman
text: If you have any clarifications, you can pose that.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Otherwise, I suggest you move on to amendments (4) to (7), please?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, can I briefly respond to Minister Indranee Rajah on her observations about the process of filing?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Not to reopen the substantive debate, but just to respond to one or two of her observations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, Ms He Ting Ru and I filed the amendments with the Clerk of Parliament on Monday.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I do understand the point the Minister is making that the Notice was sent out to all Members of Parliament on the Wednesday.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But I just want to make the point that we did file the amendments that we planned to move on the Monday.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I do also want to make the observation that we received the notification that the President's recommendation was necessary on the Saturday at about 1.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, we worked on it from that point on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I would like to move amendments (4) to (7)* standing in the Order Paper Supplement in my name.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Sorry, Mr Chairman, just a very quick response and not to belabour the matter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I understand that the Member may have put in the amendments earlier.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: All I am saying is that it would be helpful, even though the Standing Orders have a specific procedural requirement of time, that you can, of your own volition, also notify the Government ahead of time so that it would actually give us a little bit more time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, that is all I am saying, in terms of just a matter of adequate time and preparation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this case, we had taken a decision and looked at it, and decided not to put forward the recommendation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But I would just like to remind Members that one does not go to the President with less than 48 hours and say, "Here it is, please make a decision." If something was put forward, the President would have to consider it and it would take some time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But in this case, as the Government, having taken the decision, had made the decision not to put it forward for the reasons stated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just to respond to the Leader of the House, thank you for the clarification.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There was no intention to give the Government very little time to respond.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think this is a novel process insofar as at least my time in the House is concerned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think such an amendment has come up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the intention was to make sure we filed on time as per the Standing Order, which we did.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And thereafter, on the Saturday, after Mr Perera received the note from the Clerk of Parliament, I think he followed up with the Clerk of Parliament with a list of questions as to procedure and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, there was no intention to try and give the Government very little time to respond or anything of that sort.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I just thought I ought to put that on the record.

speaker: The Chairman
text: The question is as proposed by the Member.
